trait Array2[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1\]
    extends { Indexed1[\s0\], Indexed2[\s1\], Rank2,
              StandardMutableArrayType[\Array2[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1\],T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] }
    excludes { Number, String }
  getter size():ZZ32 = s0 s1
  getter sizes():(ZZ32,ZZ32) = (s0, s1)
  getter bounds():CompactFullRange2D[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] = sized2Range[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](0,0,b0,b1,s0,s1)
  getter asString(): String = do
    r : String := "[" b0 "#" s0 "," b1 "#" s1 "]"
    row(i) =
      for j <- seq(0#s1) do
         r := r " " get(i,j)
      end
    if s0 = 0 then
      r "[]"
    else
      r := r  // "["
      row(0)
      for i <- seq(1#(s0-1)) do
        r := r // " "
        row(i)
      end
      r " ]"
    end
  end
  opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0 s1
  (* Translate from b0,b1-indexing to 0-indexing, checking bounds. *)
  offset(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):(ZZ32,ZZ32) = do
    (a0,a1) = t1
    c0 = a0 - b0
    c1 = a1 - b1
    if NOT (0 <= c0 < s0) then
        oops(1,b0,s0,a0)
    elif NOT (0 <= c1 < s1) then
        oops(2,b1,s1,a1)
    else
        (c0,c1)
    end
  end
  toIndex(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):(ZZ32,ZZ32) = do (a0,a1)=t1; (a0+b0,a1+b1) end
  opr[x:ZZ32,y:ZZ32]:=(v:T):() = do self[ (x,y) ] := v end
  opr[r:Range[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]]: Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
      r' = self.bounds.narrowToRange(r)
      (z0,z1) = r'.extent.get
      (l0,l1) = r'.left.get
      (m0,m1) = r'.stride
      __subarray(self, N[\0\],reflect(z0), N[\0\], reflect(z1),
                 reflect(l0),reflect(l1),m0,m1)
    end
  opr[_:TrivialOpenRange] : Array2[\T,0,s0,0,s1\] =
      subarray[\0,s0,0,s1,b0,b1\](1,1)
  (** Indexing by pairs of ranges *)
(*
  opr[r0:Range[\ZZ32\], r1:Range[\ZZ32\]]: Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
      (r0',r1') = ((b0#s0).narrowToRange(r0), (b1#s1).narrowToRange(r1))
      (z0,z1) = (r0'.extent.get,r1'.extent.get)
      (l0,l1) = (r0'.left.get,r1'.left.get)
      (m0,m1) = (r0'.stride,r1'.stride)
      __subarray(self, N[\0\], reflect(z0), N[\0\], reflect(z1),
                 reflect(l0),reflect(l1),m0,m1)
    end
  opr[_:TrivialOpenRange, r1:Range[\ZZ32\]]: Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
      self[b0#s0,r1]
    end
  opr[r0:Range[\ZZ32\], _:TrivialOpenRange]: Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
      self[r0,b1#s1]
    end
  opr[_:TrivialOpenRange, _:TrivialOpenRange]: Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = self[:]
*)
  (** Row and column extraction *)
  opr[_:TrivialOpenRange, i1:ZZ32]: Array[\T,ZZ32\] = Col(self[(b0,i1)#(s0,1)])
(*
  opr[r:Range[\ZZ32\], i1:ZZ32]: Array[\T,ZZ32\] =        Col(self[r, i1#1])
*)
  opr[i0:ZZ32, _:TrivialOpenRange]: Array[\T,ZZ32\] = Row(self[(i0,b1)#(1,s1)])
(*
  opr[i0:ZZ32, r:Range[\ZZ32\]]: Array[\T,ZZ32\] =        Row(self[i0#1, r])
*)
  shift(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)): Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
      (o0,o1)=t1
      if o0=0 AND o1=0 then
          self
      else
          __subarray(self,reflect(o0),N[\s0\], reflect(o1),N[\s1\], N[\b0\],N[\b1\],1,1)
      end
    end

  (** 2-D subarray given static subarray parameters.
      (bo1,bo2)#(so1,so2) are output bounds.
      The result is the subarray starting at (o0,o1) in the original array,
      striding by (m0,m1).
   **)
  subarray[\nat bo0, nat so0, nat bo1, nat so1, nat o0, nat o1\]
          (m0:ZZ32,m1:ZZ32): Array2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1\] = do
      boundsCheck = self.bounds.narrowToRange( (o0,o1)::(m0,m1)#(so0,so1) )
      SubArray2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1,b0,s0,b1,s1\](self,m0,o0,m1,o1)
    end

  zeroIndices():CompactFullRange2D[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] = sized2Range[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](0,0,0,0,s0,s1)

  replica[\U\]():Array2[\U,b0,s0,b1,s1\] =
      __builtinFactory2[\U,b0,s0,b1,s1\]()
  copy():Array2[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1\] =
      self.replica[\T\]().fill(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):T => get(i-b0,j-b1))
  put(t1:(ZZ32, ZZ32), v:T) : ()
  get(t1:(ZZ32, ZZ32)):T
  t():Array2[\T,b1,s1,b0,s0\] = TransposedArray2[\T,b1,s1,b0,s0\](self)
  (* Copied here for better return type information. *)
  map[\R\](f:T->R): Array2[\R,b0,s0,b1,s1\] =
      replica[\R\]().fill(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):R => f(get(i-b0,j-b1)))
  ivmap[\R\](f:((ZZ32,ZZ32),T)->R): Array2[\R,b0,s0,b1,s1\] =
      replica[\R\]().fill(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):R => f((i,j),get(i-b0,j-b1)))

  freeze():ImmutableArray[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = fail("Freeze not defined yet!")
end

(** Hoisted out here to work around the lack of method type inference. **)
__subarray[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1,
           nat bo0, nat so0, nat bo1, nat so1, nat o0, nat o1\]
        (this:Array2[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1\],
         _:N[\bo0\],_:N[\so0\],_:N[\bo1\],_:N[\so1\],
         _:N[\o0\],_:N[\o1\],m0:ZZ32,m1:ZZ32): Array2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1\] = do
    this.subarray[\bo0,so0,bo1,so1,o0,o1\](m0,m1)
  end

(** Default array is column-major, but we could switch it. **)
object __DefaultArray2[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1\]()
        extends Array2[\T, b0, s0, b1, s1\]
    mem:PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \] = PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \]()
    init0(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.init0(i s1 + j, v) end
    put(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.put(i s1 + j, v) end
    get(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):T = do (i,j)=t1; mem.get(i s1 + j) end
end

(** Transposes the index of the underlying array mem, and transposes
    its natural order as well. **)
object TransposedArray2[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1\]
                       (mem:Array2[\T,b1,s1,b0,s0\])
    extends Array2[\T, b0, s0, b1, s1\]
  replica[\U\]():Array2[\U,b0,s0,b1,s1\] = mem.replica[\U\]().t()

  init0(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.init0((j,i),v) end
  put(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.put((j,i),v) end
  get(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):T = do (i,j)=t1; mem.get(j,i) end
  t():Array2[\T,b1,s1,b0,s0\] = mem
  (** 2-D subarray given static subarray parameters.
      (bo1,bo2)#(so1,so2) are output bounds.
      The result is the subarray starting at (o0,o1) in the original array,
      striding by (m0,m1).
   **)
  subarray[\nat bo0, nat so0, nat bo1, nat so1, nat o0, nat o1\]
          (m0:ZZ32,m1:ZZ32): Array2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1\] =
      mem.subarray[\bo1,so1,bo0,so0,o1,o0\](m1,m0).t()
end

(** Simple 2-D subarray, used when we have no other knowledge of the
    underlying structure.  If we're on top of a PrimitiveArray we can
    really do much better than this.
    (b0,b1)#(s0,s1) are the bounds of the subarray.
    (bu0,bu1)#(su0,su1) are the bounds of the underlying array.
    m_i, o_i are multiplier and offset (0-based) of dimension i.
**)
object SubArray2[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1,
                     nat bu0, nat su0, nat bu1, nat su1\]
                (mem: Array2[\T,bu0,su0,bu1,su1\],
                 m0:ZZ32, o0:ZZ32, m1:ZZ32, o1:ZZ32)
        extends Array2[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1\]
    index(a0:ZZ32, a1:ZZ32): (ZZ32,ZZ32) = (m0 a0 + o0, m1 a1 + o1)
    init0(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T): () = mem.init0(index(t1),v)
    put(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T): () = mem.put(index(t1),v)
    get(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)): T = mem.get(index(t1))
    (** 2-D subarray given static subarray parameters.
        (bo1,bo2)#(so1,so2) are output bounds.
        The result is the subarray starting at (o0,o1) in the original array,
        striding by (m0,m1).
     **)
    subarray[\nat bo0, nat so0, nat bo1, nat so1, nat on0, nat on1\]
            (mn0:ZZ32,mn1:ZZ32): Array2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1\] = do
        boundsCheck = self.bounds.narrowToRange( (on0,on1)::(mn0,mn1)#(so0,so1) )
        (o0', o1') = index(on0 - bo0, on1 - bo1)
        SubArray2[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1,bu0,su0,bu1,su1\](mem,mn0,o0',mn1,o1')
      end
end

object Col[\T, nat b0, nat s0\](mem: Array2[\T,b0,s0,0,1\])
        extends Array1[\T,b0,s0\]
    get(i:ZZ32): T = mem.get(i,0)
    put(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.put((i,0),v)
    init0(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.init0((i,0),v)
    offset(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r,_) = mem.offset(i,0); r end
    toIndex(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r,_) = mem.toIndex(i,0); r end
    subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m: ZZ32): ReadableArray1[\T, b, s\] =
        Col[\T,b,s\](mem.subarray[\b,s,0,1,o,0\](m,1))
end

object Row[\T, nat b1, nat s1\](mem: Array2[\T,0,1,b1,s1\])
        extends Array1[\T,b1,s1\]
    get(i:ZZ32): T = mem.get(0,i)
    put(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.put((0,i),v)
    init0(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.init0((0,i),v)
    offset(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (_,r) = mem.offset(0,i); r end
    toIndex(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (_,r) = mem.toIndex(0,i); r end
    subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m: ZZ32): ReadableArray1[\T, b, s\] =
        Row[\T,b,s\](mem.subarray[\0,1,b,s,0,o\](1,m))
end

trait AnyMatrix end

trait Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]
        extends { AnyMatrix, Array2[\T, 0, s0, 0, s1\], AdditiveGroup[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\] }
        excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    opr +(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e + v.get(i))
    opr -(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e - v.get(i))
    opr -(self): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => - e)
    scale(t1: T): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => t1 e)
    mul[\ nat s2 \](other: Matrix[\T,s1,s2\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s2\] = do
        res = matrix[\T,s0,s2\]()
        mma(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)
                (* If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition. *)
                res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                (mma(a,i,b,j,c,k0),mma(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1))
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mma(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                (mma(a,i0,b,j,c,k),mma(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k))
            end
        mm(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                res.put((a,c), get(a,b) other.get(b,c))
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                (mm(a,i,b,j,c,k0),mm(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1))
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mm(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                (mm(a,i0,b,j,c,k),mm(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k))
            end
        if s0=0 OR s1=0 OR s2=0 then
          res
        else
          mm(0,s0,0,s1,0,s2)
          res
        end
      end
    rmul(v: Vector[\T,s1\]): Vector[\T,s0\] = do
        row(i:ZZ32):T =
            SUM[(j,v_j)<-v.indexValuePairs] get(i,j) v_j
        vector[\T,s0\]().fill(row)
      end
    lmul(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s1\] = do
        col(i:ZZ32):T =
            SUM[(j,v_j)<-v.indexValuePairs] v_j get(j,i)
        vector[\T,s1\]().fill(col)
      end
    t(): Matrix[\T,s1,s0\] = TransposedMatrix[\T,s1,s0\](self)
end

(* Default matrix should match default array in column vs row-major. *)
object __DefaultMatrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]()
    extends Matrix[\T, s0, s1\]
  mem:PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \] = PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \]()
  init0(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.init0(i s1 + j, v) end
  put(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = do (i,j)=t1; mem.put(i s1 + j, v) end
  get(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):T = do (i,j)=t1; mem.get(i s1 + j) end
end

object TransposedMatrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\](mem:Matrix[\T,s1,s0\])
        extends Matrix[\T, s0, s1\]

trait Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]

    opr -(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e - v.get(i))
    opr -(self): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => - e)
    scale(t1: T): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => t1 e)
    mul[\ nat s2 \](other: Matrix[\T,s1,s2\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s2\] = do
        res = matrix[\T,s0,s2\]()
        mma(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)
                (* If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition. *)
                res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                (mma(a,i,b,j,c,k0),mma(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1))
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mma(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                (mma(a,i0,b,j,c,k),mma(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k))
            end
        mm(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                res.put((a,c), get(a,b) other.get(b,c))
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                (mm(a,i,b,j,c,k0),mm(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1))
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mm(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                (mm(a,i0,b,j,c,k),mm(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k))
            end
        if s0=0 OR s1=0 OR s2=0 then
          res
        else
          mm(0,s0,0,s1,0,s2)
          res
        end
      end
    rmul(v: Vector[\T,s1\]): Vector[\T,s0\] = do
        row(i:ZZ32):T =
            SUM[(j,v_j)<-v.indexValuePairs] get(i,j) v_j
        vector[\T,s0\]().fill(row)
      end
    lmul(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s1\] = do
        col(i:ZZ32):T =
            SUM[(j,v_j)<-v.indexValuePairs] v_j get(j,i)
        vector[\T,s1\]().fill(col)
      end

   matrix elements. *)
opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\]
       (me:Matrix[\T,n,m\], other:Matrix[\T,m,p\]): Matrix[\T,n,p\] =
        me.mul[\p\](other)

opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\]
     (me:Matrix[\T,n,m\], other:Matrix[\T,m,p\]): Matrix[\T,n,p\] =
        me.mul[\p\](other)


(* matrix-vector multiplication *)
opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
       (me:Matrix[\T,n,m\], v:Vector[\T,m\]):Vector[\T,n\] = me.rmul(v)

opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
     (me:Matrix[\T,n,m\], v:Vector[\T,m\]):Vector[\T,n\] = me.rmul(v)

(* vector-matrix multiplication *)
opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
       (v:Vector[\T,n\], me:Matrix[\T,n,m\]):Vector[\T,m\] = me.lmul(v)

opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
     (v:Vector[\T,n\], me:Matrix[\T,n,m\]):Vector[\T,m\] = me.lmul(v)

opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
       (me : Matrix[\T,n,m\], other : T) : Matrix[\T,n,m\] = me.scale(other)

opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
     (me : Matrix[\T,n,m\], other : T) : Matrix[\T,n,m\] = me.scale(other)

opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
       (other : T, me : Matrix[\T,n,m\]) : Matrix[\T,n,m\] = me.scale(other)

opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
     (other : T, me : Matrix[\T,n,m\]) : Matrix[\T,n,m\] = me.scale(other)

(** Array3[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\] is the type of 3-dimensional arrays
    of element type T, with size s_i in the i^th dimension and lowest
    index (b0,b1,b2).  Natural order for all generators in each

   is just Fortress overloading (r04_glyphs.out: × ÷ - ⊖ ⊂ ⊃ ≡ ≢ * and ∘ all
   take a prefix AND an infix declaration; , ⌈ ⌊ do not). *)

    85	operator? Doing so requires having a special constant value for e.}
    86	
    87	\subsection{Superscript Operators}
    88	
    89	The superscript operator \EXP{\txt{\char'136}\VAR{T}} transposes a
    90	matrix. It also converts a column vector to a row vector or a row
    91	vector to a column vector.
    92	
    93	\subsection{Subscript Operators}
    94	
    95	Subscripting of arrays and other aggregates is written using square brackets:
    96	
    97	\begin{tabular}{llll}
    98	\txt{a[i]}        & \emph{is displayed as} & \EXP{a_i}
    99	& $i$th element of one-dimensional array \VAR{a} \\
   100	\txt{m[i,j]}      & \emph{is displayed as} &    \EXP{m_{ij}}
   101	& ${i,j}$th element  of two-dimensional matrix \VAR{m} \\
   102	\txt{space[i,j,k]}   & \emph{is displayed as} & \EXP{\VAR{space}_{ijk}}
   103	& $i,j,k$th element of three-dimensional array \VAR{space} \\
   104	\txt{a[3] := 4}      & \emph{is displayed as}
   105	& \EXP{a_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}}= 4}
   106	& assign \EXP{4} to the third element of mutable array \VAR{a} \\
   107	\txt{m["foo"]}       & \emph{is displayed as}
   108	& \EXP{m_{\hbox{\rm``{\tt foo}''}}}
   109	& fetch the entry associated with string \EXP{\hbox{\rm``{\tt foo}''}}
   110	from map \VAR{m}
   111	\end{tabular}
   112	
   113	\subsection{Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators}
   114	
   115	For most integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions,
   116	multiplication can be expressed using any of `\EXP{\cdot}' or
   117	`\EXP{\times}' or simply juxtaposition.
   118	However,
   119	the \EXP{\times} operator is used to
   120	express the shape of matrices, so if expressions using multiplication are used
   121	in expressing the shape of a matrix, it may be necessary to avoid the
   122	use of '\EXP{\times}' to
   123	express multiplication, or to use parentheses.
   124	
   125	For integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions, division is expressed by \EXP{/}.
   126	When the operator \EXP{/} is used to divide one integer by another,
   127	the result is rational.
   128	The operator \EXP{\div} performs truncating integer division:
   129	\EXP{m \div n = \mathit{signum}\left({m \over n}\right) \left\lfloor \left| {m \over n} \right| \right\rfloor}.
   130	The operator \OPR{REM} gives the remainder from such a truncating division:
   131	\EXP{m \OPR{REM} n = m - n (m \div n)}.
   132	The operator \OPR{MOD} gives the remainder from a floor division:
   133	\EXP{m \OPR{MOD} n = m - n \left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor};
   134	when \EXP{n>0} this is the usual modulus computation that evaluates integer \VAR{m}
   135	to an integer \VAR{k} such that \EXP{0\leq{}k<n} and \VAR{n} evenly divides \EXP{m-k}.
   136	
   137	The special operators \OPR{DIVREM} and \OPR{DIVMOD} each return a pair of values,
   138	the quotient and the remainder; \EXP{m \OPR{DIVREM} n} returns
   139	\EXP{(m \div n, m \OPR{REM} n)} while
   140	\EXP{m \OPR{DIVMOD} n} returns
   141	\EXP{(\left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor, m \OPR{MOD} n)}.
   142	
   143	Multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is done with juxtaposition,
   144	as is multiplication of a vector by a matrix (on either side).  Vector dot product
   145	is expressed by `\EXP{\cdot}' and vector cross product by
   146	`\EXP{\times}'.  Division of
   147	a matrix or vector by a scalar may be expressed using `\EXP{/}'.
   148	
   149	The syntactic interaction of juxtaposition, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{\times},
   150	and \EXP{/} is subtle.
   151	\See{operator-precedence} for a discussion of the relative precedence of
   152	these operations and how precedence may depend on the use of whitespace.
   153	
   154	The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
   155	For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
   156	Rational computations do not overflow.
   157	For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
   158	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
   159	For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.
   160	
   161	Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
   162	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
   163	
   164	The handling of division by zero depends on the type of the number produced.
   165	For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
   166	For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
   167	For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
   168	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
   169	For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
   170	(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).
   171	
   172	Wraparound multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
   173	\EXP{\dottimes}.
   174	Saturating multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
   175	\EXP{\boxdot} or \EXP{\boxtimes}.
   176	These operations do not overflow.
   177	
   178	Ordinary multiplication and division of floating-point numbers always
   179	use the IEEE 754 ``round to nearest'' rounding mode.  This rounding
   180	mode may be emphasized by using the operators \EXP{\otimes} (or \EXP{\odot})
   181	and \EXP{\oslash}.  Multiplication and division in ``round toward zero''
   182	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\boxtimes} (or \EXP{\boxdot}) and
   183	\EXP{\boxslash}.
   184	Multiplication and division in ``round toward positive infinity''
   185	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\uptimes} (or \EXP{\updot}) and \EXP{\upslash}.
   186	Multiplication and division in ``round toward negative infinity''
   187	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downtimes} (or \EXP{\downdot}) and
   188	\EXP{\downslash}.
   189	
   190	\subsection{Addition and Subtraction Operators}
   191	
   192	Addition and subtraction are expressed with \EXP{+} and \EXP{-} on all numeric quantities,
   193	including intervals, as well as vectors and matrices.
   194	
   195	The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
   196	For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
   197	Rational computations do not overflow.
   198	For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
   199	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
   200	For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.
   201	
   202	Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
   203	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
   204	
   205	Wraparound addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are
   206	expressed by \EXP{\dotplus} and \EXP{\dotminus}.
   207	Saturating addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are
   208	expressed by \EXP{\boxplus} and \EXP{\boxminus}.
   209	These operations do not overflow.
   210	
   211	Ordinary addition and subtraction of floating-point numbers always
   212	use the IEEE 754 ``round to nearest'' rounding mode.  This rounding
   213	mode may be emphasized by using the operators \EXP{\oplus}
   214	and \EXP{\ominus}.  Addition and subtraction in ``round toward zero''
   215	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\boxplus} and \EXP{\boxminus}.
   216	Addition and subtraction in ``round toward positive infinity''
   217	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\upplus} and \EXP{\upminus}.
   218	Addition and subtraction in ``round toward negative infinity''
   219	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downplus} and \EXP{\downminus}.
   220	
   221	The construction \EXP{x \pm y} produces the interval \EXP{\bsINT{x-y,x+y}}.
   222	
   223	\subsection{Intersection, Union, and Set Difference Operators}
   224	
   225	Sets support the operations of intersection \EXP{\cap}, union
   226	\EXP{\cup}, disjoint union \EXP{\uplus},
   227	set difference \EXP{\setminus}, and symmetric set difference
   228	\EXP{\ominus}.  Disjoint union
   229	throws \TYP{DisjointUnionError} if the arguments are in fact not disjoint.
   230	
   231	Intervals support the operations of intersection \EXP{\cap}, union
   232	\EXP{\cup}, and interior hull \EXP{\underline{\union}}.
   233	The operation \EXP{\Cap} returns a pair of intervals; if the intersection of
   234	the arguments is a single contiguous span of real numbers, then the first result is an
   235	interval representing that span and the second result is an empty interval,
   236	but if the intersection is two spans, then two (disjoint) intervals are returned.
   237	The operation \EXP{\Cup} returns a pair of intervals; if the arguments overlap, then
   238	the first result is the union of the two intervals and the second result is an empty interval,
   239	but if the arguments are disjoint, they are simply returned as is.
   240	
   241	\subsection{Minimum and Maximum Operators}
   242	
   243	The operator \OPR{MAX} returns the larger of its two operands,
   244	and \OPR{MIN} returns the smaller of its two operands.
   245	
   246	For floating-point numbers, if either argument is a \TYP{NaN} then
   247	\TYP{NaN} is returned.  The floating-point operations \OPR{MAXNUM} and
   248	\OPR{MINNUM}
   249	behave similarly except that if one argument is \TYP{NaN} and the
   250	other is a number, the number is returned.  For all four of these
   251	operators, when applied to floating-point values,
   252	\EXP{-0} is considered to be smaller than \EXP{+0}.
   253	
   254	\subsection{GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators}
   255	
   256	The infix operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common
   257	divisor of its integer operands, and \OPR{LCM} computes the least
   258	common multiple.  The operator \OPR{CHOOSE} computes binomial
   259	coefficients:
   260	\EXP{n \OPR{CHOOSE} k = \binom{n}{k} = { n! \over k!(n-k)! }}.
   261	
   262	The expression \EXP{e \neq e'} is semantically equivalent to the expression
   263	\EXP{\neg(e = e')}.
   264	
   265	
   266	\subsection{Comparisons Operators}
   267	
   268	Unless otherwise noted, the operators described in this section
   269	produce boolean (\VAR{true}/\VAR{false}) results.
   270	
   271	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and $>$ are
   272	  used for numerical comparisons
   273	and are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types.
   274	Comparison of rational values throws \TYP{RationalComparisonError}
   275	if either argument is the rational infinity \EXP{1/0} or the
   276	rational indefinite \EXP{0/0}.
   277	Comparison of floating-point values throws \TYP{FloatingComparisonError}
   278	if either argument is a \TYP{NaN}.
   279	
   280	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} may also be
   281	used to compare characters
   282	(according to the numerical value of their Unicode codepoint values)
   283	and strings (lexicographic order based on the character ordering).
   284	They also use lexicographic order when used to compare lists
   285	whose elements support these same comparison operators.
   286	
   287	When $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} are used to compare numerical
   288	intervals, the result is a boolean interval.  The functions
   289	\VAR{possibly} and \VAR{certainly} are useful for converting
   290	boolean intervals to boolean values for testing.  Thus
   291	\EXP{\VAR{possibly}(x>y)} is true if and only if there is some value in the interval
   292	\VAR{x} that is greater than some value in the interval \VAR{y}, while
   293	\EXP{\VAR{certainly}(x>y)} is true if and only if \VAR{x} and \VAR{y} are nonempty
   294	and every value in \VAR{x} is greater than every value in \VAR{y}.
   295	
   296	The operators \EXP{\subset}, \EXP{\subseteq}, \EXP{\supseteq}, and
   297	\EXP{\supset} may be used to compare sets or intervals regarded as sets.
   298	
   299	The operator \EXP{\in} may be used to test whether a value is a member of
   300	a set, list, array, interval, or range.
   301	
   302	\subsection{Logical Operators}
   303	
   304	The following binary operators may be used on boolean values:
   305	\begin{center}
   306	\begin{tabular}{rl}
   307	$\wedge$ & \scap{and} \\
   308	$\vee$ & inclusive \scap{or} \\
   309	$\underline{\vee}$ or $\oplus$ or $\neq$ & exclusive \scap{or} \\
   310	$\equiv$ or $\leftrightarrow$ or $=$ & equivalence (if and only if) \\
   311	$\rightarrow$ & \scap{implies} \\
   312	$\overline{\wedge}$ & \scap{nand} \\
   313	$\overline{\vee}$ & \scap{nor}
   314	\end{tabular}
   315	\end{center}
   316	
   317	These same operators may also be applied to boolean intervals
   318	to produce boolean interval results.
   319	
   320	The following operators may be used on integers to perform
   321	``bitwise'' operations:
   322	\begin{center}
   323	\begin{tabular}{rl}
   324	$\twointersectand$ & bitwise \scap{and} \\
   325	$\twointersector$ & bitwise inclusive \scap{or} \\
   326	$\underline{\twointersector}$ & bitwise exclusive \scap{or}
   327	\end{tabular}
   328	\end{center}
   329	The prefix operator \EXP{\twointersectnot} computes the bitwise
   330	\scap{not} of an integer.
   331	
   332	
   333	\subsection{Conditional Operators}
   334	\seclabel{standard-conditional-oprs}
   335	
   336	If \EXP{p(x)} and \EXP{q(x)} are expressions that produce
   337	boolean results, the expression \EXP{p(x) \wedge\mathpunct{\mathtt{:}}
   338	  q(x)} computes the
   339	logical \scap{and} of those two results by first evaluating \EXP{p(x)}.
   340	If the result of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{true}, then \EXP{q(x)} is also
   341	evaluated, and its
   342	result becomes the result of the entire expression; but if the result
   343	of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{false}, then \EXP{q(x)} is not evaluated,
   344	and the result of the entire expression is \VAR{false} without further ado.
   345	(Similarly, evaluating the expression \EXP{p(x)
   346	  \vee\mathpunct{\mathtt{:}} q(x)} does not
   347	evaluate \EXP{q(x)} if the result of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{true}.)
   348	Contrast this with the expression \EXP{p(x) \wedge q(x)} (with no colon),
   349	which evaluates both \EXP{p(x)} and \EXP{q(x)}, in no specified order and
   350	possibly in parallel.

    12	\section{Operator Names}

    16	Operator names are either operator tokens or special operator characters,
    17	or a few reserved words.}
    18	
    19	To support a rich mathematical notation, Fortress allows most Unicode
    20	characters
    21	that are specified to be mathematical operators to be used as operators in
    22	Fortress expressions, as well as these characters:
    23	\begin{ttt}
    24	!~~~{\char'100}~~~{\char'43}~~~{\char'44}~~~{\char'45}~~~*~~~+~~~-~~~=~~~{\char'174}~~~:~~~<~~~>~~~/~~~?~~~{\char'136}~~~{\verb+~+} \\
    25	->~~~-->~~~=>~~~==>~~~<=~~~>=~~~=/=~~~!!~~~{\char'174}{\char'174}~~~{\char'174}{\char'174}{\char'174}\\

    27	\end{ttt}
    28	In addition, a token that is made up of a mixture of uppercase letters and underscores
    29	(but no digits), does not begin or end with an underscore, and contains at least two
    30	different letters is also considered to be an operator:

    32	MAX~~~MIN
    33	\end{ttt}

    12	\section{Operator Fixity}
    13	\seclabel{operator-fixity}
    14	
    15	\note{Multifix operators are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	Most operators in Fortress can be used variously as prefix, postfix,
    18	infix, nofix, or multifix operators.
    19	(See \secref{chained-multifix} for a discussion of how
    20	infix operators may be chained
    21	or treated as multifix operators.)
    22	\note{
    23	Victor: I think that we shouldn't list ``multifix'' separately here.
    24	 (Note that multifix does not appear in any of the tables.)
    25	 Rather multifix is a way to interpret infix operators.}
    26	Some operators can be used in pairs
    27	as enclosing (bracketing) operators---see \secref{enclosing-ops}.
    28	The Fortress language
    29	dictates only the rules of syntax; whether an operator has
    30	a meaning when used in a particular way depends only on whether
    31	there is a definition in the program for that operator when
    32	used in that particular way (see \chapref{operatordefs}).
    33	
    34	The fixity of a non-enclosing operator is determined by context.
    35	To the left of such an operator we may find
    36	(1) a \emph{primary tail} (described below),
    37	(2) another operator, or
    38	(3) a comma, semicolon, or left encloser.  To the right we may find
    39	(1) a \emph{primary front} (described below),
    40	(2) another operator, (3) a comma, semicolon, or right
    41	encloser, or (4) a line break.
    42	%
    43	A primary tail is an identifier, a literal,
    44	a right encloser, or a superscripted postfix operator (exponent operator).
    45	A primary front is an identifier, a literal, or a left encloser.
    46	%
    47	\note{
    48	A primary expression is an identifier, a literal,
    49	an expression enclosed by matching enclosers, a field selection,
    50	or an expression followed by a postfix operator.}
    51	Considered in all combinations, this makes twelve possibilities.
    52	In some cases one must also consider whether or not whitespace separates the operator
    53	from what lies on either side.  The rules of operator fixity are specified
    54	by \figref{opr-fixity1}, where the center column indicates the fixity that results
    55	from the left and right context specified by the other columns.

    88	\figlabel{opr-fixity1}
    89	\end{figure}
    90	
    91	A case described in the center column of the table as an {\bf error}
    92	is a static error; for such cases, the fixity mentioned in parentheses
    93	is the recommended treatment of the operator for the purpose of
    94	attempting to continuing the parse in search of other errors.
    95	
    96	The table may seem complicated, but it all boils down to a couple of practical rules of thumb:
    97	\begin{enumerate}
    98	\item {\it Any} operator can be prefix, postfix, infix, or nofix.
    99	
   100	\item An infix operator can be \emph{loose} (having whitespace on both sides)
   101	or \emph{tight} (having whitespace on neither side), but it mustn't be \emph{lopsided}
   102	(having whitespace on one side but not the other).
   103	
   104	\item A postfix operator must have no whitespace before it and must
   105	be followed (possibly after some whitespace) by a comma, semicolon, right encloser, or line break.

    11	
    12	\section{Juxtaposition}
    13	\seclabel{juxtameaning}
    14	
    15	\note{Qualified names are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	Juxtaposition in Fortress may be a function call or
    18	a special infix operator.  \Library\ include several declarations of
    19	a \KWD{juxtaposition} operator.
    20	
    21	When two expressions are juxtaposed, the juxtaposition is interpreted as
    22	follows:
    23	if the left-hand-side expression is a function, juxtaposition performs
    24	function application;
    25	otherwise, juxtaposition performs the
    26	\KWD{juxtaposition} operator application.
    27	
    28	The manner in which a juxtaposition of three or more items must be associated
    29	requires type information and awareness of whitespace.  (This is an inherent property
    30	of customary mathematical notation, which Fortress is designed to emulate where feasible.)
    31	Therefore a Fortress compiler must produce a provisional parse in which such
    32	multi-element juxtapositions are held in abeyance, then perform a type analysis
    33	on each element and use that information to rewrite the n-ary juxtaposition
    34	into a tree of binary juxtapositions.
    35	
    36	All we need to know is whether each element of a
    37	juxtaposition has an arrow type.
    38	There are actually three legitimate possibilities for each element of a juxtaposition:
    39	(a) it has an arrow type, in which case it is considered to be a function
    40	element;
    41	(b) it has a type that is not an arrow type, in which case it is considered
    42	to be a non-function element.
    43	(c) it is an identifier that has no visible declaration,
    44	in which case it is considered to be a function element (and everything will work
    45	out okay if it turns out to be the name of an appropriate functional method).
    46	
    47	The rules below are designed to forbid certain forms of notational ambiguity
    48	that can arise if the name of a functional method happens to be used also
    49	as the name of a variable.  For example, suppose that trait \VAR{T} has a functional
    50	method of one parameter named \VAR{n}; then in the code
    51	%% do
    52	%%   a: T = t
    53	%%   n: ZZ = 14

    38	we show how to determine which declarations
    39	are applicable to a \emph{named functional call}
    40	(a function call described in \secref{function-calls}
    41	or a naked method invocation described in \secref{naked-method-calls})
    42	when all declarations have only ordinary parameters
    43	(without varargs or keyword
    44	parameters).
    45	We discuss how to handle dotted method calls
    46	(described in \secref{dotted-method-calls})
    47	in \secref{dotted-method-applicability},
    48	and declarations with varargs and keyword

    54	
    55	\section{Principles of Overloading}
    56	\seclabel{overloading-terms}
    57	
    58	Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
    59	be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
    60	the following shadowing rules:
    61	\begin{itemize}
    62	\item
    63	dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
    64	the same name, and
    65	\item
    66	dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
    67	or object expression
    68	shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
    69	provided by a different trait or object declaration
    70	or object expression.
    71	\end{itemize}
    72	Also, note that a trait or object declaration
    73	or object expression must not have a
    74	functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
    75	same name, either directly or by inheritance.
    76	Therefore, top-level functions can overload
    77	with other top-level functions and functional methods,
    78	dotted methods with other dotted methods,
    79	and functional methods with other functional methods and top-level functions.
    80	It is a static error if any top-level function declaration is
    81	more specific than any functional method declaration.
    82	If a top-level function declaration is overloaded with a functional method
    83	declaration, the top-level function declaration must not be more specific than
    84	the functional method declaration.
    85	
    86	
    87	Operator declarations with the same name but different fixity
    88	are not a valid overloading; they are unambiguous declarations.
    89	An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
    90	(described in \secref{opr-ident})
    91	of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
    92	declarations in the same component.
    93	Therefore, such an operator method declaration
    94	must satisfy the overloading rules
    95	(described in \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
    96	with every operator declaration in the same component.
    97	
    98	\note{This restriction will be relaxed.}
    99	
   100	Although there may be multiple declarations
   101	with the same functional name,
   102	it is an error for their static parameters to differ
   103	(up to $\alpha$-equivalence),
   104	or for one declaration to have static parameters
   105	and another to not have them.
   106	Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
   107	declarations are applicable,
   108	so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
   109	
   110	
   111	
   112	Recall from \chapref{types} that we write
   113	$T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
   114	and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$.
   115	
   116	
   117	\section{Applicability to Named Functional Calls}
   118	\seclabel{functional-applicability}
   119	In this section, we show how to determine which declarations are
   120	applicable to a named functional call when all declarations have only
   121	ordinary parameters (i.e., neither varargs nor keyword parameters).
   122	
   123	For the purpose of defining applicability, a named functional call can
   124	be characterized by the name of the functional and its argument type.
   125	Recall that a functional has a single parameter, which may be a tuple
   126	(a dotted method has a receiver as well).
   127	 We abuse notation by using
   128	\emph{static call $\f(\As)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   129	name $\f$ and whose argument has static type $\As$, and
   130	\emph{dynamic call $\f(\Xs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   131	We use \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   132	name $\f$ and whose argument, when evaluated, has dynamic type $\Cs$.
   133	(Note that if the type system is sound---and we certainly hope that
   134	it is!---then $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \As$ for all well-typed calls to $\f$.)
   135	We use the term \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to static and dynamic calls
   136	collectively.
   137	We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
   138	have been instantiated or inferred.
   139	
   140	
   141	We also use \emph{function declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$} to refer to a
   142	function declaration with function name $\f$, parameter type $\Ps$,
   143	and return type $\Us$.
   144	
   145	
   146	For method declarations, we must take into account the self parameter,
   147	as follows:
   148	
   149	A \emph{dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps):\Us$} is a dotted
   150	method declaration with name $f$, where $\Ps_0$ is the trait or object
   151	type in which the declaration appears, $\Ps$ is the parameter type,
   152	and $\Us$ is the return type.  (Note that despite the suggestive
   153	notation, a dotted method declaration does not explicitly list its
   154	self parameter.)
   155	
   156	A \emph{functional method declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$ with self
   157	parameter at $i$} is a functional method declaration with name $f$,
   158	with the parameter \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}} in the $i$th position
   159	of the parameter type $\Ps$, and return type $\Us$.  Note that the static
   160	type of the self parameter is the trait or object trait type in which
   161	the declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$ occurs.  In the following, we will use
   162	$\Ps_i$ to refer to the $i$th element of $\Ps$.
   163	
   164	We elide the return type of a declaration, writing $\f(\Ps)$ and
   165	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$, when the return type is not relevant to the
   166	discussion.
   167	Note that static parameters may appear in the types $\Ps_0$, $\Ps$, and $\Us$.
   168	
   169	
   170	A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable} to a call $\f(\Cs)$
   171	if the call is in the scope of the declaration and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   172	(See \chapref{names} for the definition of scope.)
   173	If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters,
   174	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   175	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   176	
   177	
   178	
   179	Note that a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ may invoke a dotted method
   180	declaration if the declaration is provided by the trait or object
   181	enclosing the call.  To account for this, let $\Cs_0$ be the trait or
   182	object declaration immediately enclosing the call.
   183	%
   184	Then we consider a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ as $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$
   185	if $\Cs_0$ provides dotted method declarations applicable to $\f(\Cs)$, and
   186	use the rule for applicability to dotted method calls (described in
   187	\secref{dotted-method-applicability}) to determine which declarations
   188	are applicable to $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$.
   189	
   190	
   191	
   192	\section{Applicability to Dotted Method Calls}
   193	\seclabel{dotted-method-applicability}
   194	
   195	Dotted method applications can be characterized similarly to named
   196	functional applications, except that, analogously to dotted method declarations,
   197	we use $\Cs_0$ to denote the dynamic type of the receiver object,
   198	and, as for named functional calls, $\Cs$ to denote the dynamic
   199	type of the argument of a  dotted method call.
   200	We write $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ to refer to the  call.
   201	
   202	A dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable}
   203	to a dotted method call $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype
   204	\Ps_0$ and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   205	If the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ include static parameters,
   206	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   207	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   208	
   209	
   210	
   211	\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
   212	\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}
   213	
   214	The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
   215	parameters is that we
   216	can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
   217	though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
   218	set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
   219	these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
   220	of arguments that can be passed to it.
   221	
   222	
   223	A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
   224	number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
   225	passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
   226	number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
   227	called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
   228	will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
   229	arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
   230	simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
   231	implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
   232	%
   233	For example, the following declaration:
   234	%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z : ZZ...):ZZ
   235	\begin{Fortress}
   236	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
   237	\end{Fortress}
   238	would be expanded into:
   239	%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ):ZZ
   240	%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ):ZZ
   241	%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ):ZZ
   242	%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ, z3 : ZZ):ZZ
   243	%...
   244	\begin{Fortress}
   245	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   246	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   247	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   248	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   249	\(\ldots\)
   250	\end{Fortress}
   251	A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
   252	any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.
   253	
   254	
   255	
   256	\section{Overloading Resolution}
   257	\seclabel{resolving-overloading}
   258	
   259	\note{
   260	Victor: Does this paragraph, other than the last sentence,
   261	really belong in this section?}
   262	
   263	To evaluate a given functional call,
   264	it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
   265	to dispatch to.
   266	To do so,
   267	we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
   268	If there is exactly one such declaration,
   269	then the call dispatches to that declaration.
   270	If there is no such declaration,
   271	then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
   272	(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
   273	for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
   274	If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
   275	then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
   276	no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
   277	
   278	
   279	
   280	We use the subtype relation to compare parameter types to determine
   281	a more specific declaration.
   282	Formally, a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than a declaration
   283	$\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.  Similarly, a declaration
   284	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is more specific than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$
   285	if $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$ and $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.
   286	(See \secref{resolving-coercion} for how coercion
   287	changes the definition of ``more specific''.)
   288	Restrictions on the definition of overloaded functionals
   289	(see \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
   290	guarantee that among all applicable declarations,
   291	one is more specific than all the others.
   292	If the declarations include static parameters,
   293	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   294	before comparing their parameter types
   295	to determine which declaration is more specific.

    12	\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{reduction-expr}

    15	\begin{Grammar}
    16	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
    17	\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    18	\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\
    19	
    20	\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
    21	\end{Grammar}
    22	
    23	A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
    24	$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
    25	an optional generator clause list (described in
    26	\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
    27	There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
    28	\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
    29	\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
    30	%% opr BIG Op[\T\](g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0):R
    31	\begin{Fortress}
    32	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
    33	\end{Fortress}
    34	Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
    35	the method %generate[\R0\]
    36	\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
    37	of the trait %Generator[\T\]
    38	\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
    39	it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
    40	\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
    41	and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
    42	and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
    43	generated element and combining them using the reduction.
    44	When a generator clause
    45	list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
    46	identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
    47	body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
    48	thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
    49	combined together using \emph{Op}
    50	\label{redexpr-redvar}
    51	as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
    52	The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.

    54	object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are

    12	\section{Generators}
    13	\seclabel{generators}
    14	
    15	\note{Distributions are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\begin{Grammar}
    18	\emph{GeneratorClauseList} &::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding}(\EXP{,} \emph{GeneratorClause})$^*$ \\
    19	
    20	\emph{GeneratorBinding}
    21	&::=& \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}\EXP{\leftarrow}\emph{Expr} \\
    22	
    23	\emph{GeneratorClause}
    24	&::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding} \\
    25	&$|$& \emph{Expr} \\
    26	
    27	\emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}
    28	&::=& \emph{BindId}\\
    29	&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}\EXP{,} \emph{BindIdList} \texttt{)}\\
    30	
    31	\emph{BindIdList} &::=& \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^*$\\
    32	
    33	\emph{BindId} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
    34	&$|$& \KWD{\_}\\
    35	\end{Grammar}
    36	
    37	Fortress makes extensive use of comma-separated \emph{generator clause lists}
    38	to express parallel iteration.  Generator clause lists occur in
    39	generated expressions (described in \secref{generated}) and
    40	\KWD{for} loops (described in \secref{for-expr}),
    41	sums and big operators (described in \secref{reduction-expr}),
    42	and comprehensions (described in \secref{comprehensions}).
    43	We refer to these
    44	collectively as \emph{expressions with generator clauses}.  Every expression with
    45	generator clauses contains a \emph{body expression} which is evaluated for each
    46	combination of values bound in the generator clause list
    47	(each such combination yields an \emph{iteration} of the body).
    48	
    49	A generator clause is either a \emph{generator binding} or
    50	an expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket}
    51	(this includes the type \TYP{Boolean}).
    52	A generator clause list must begin with a generator binding.
    53	A generator binding consists of one or more
    54	comma-separated identifiers followed by the token \EXP{\leftarrow},
    55	followed by a subexpression (called the \emph{generator expression}).
    56	A generator expression evaluates to an object whose type is
    57	\TYP{Generator}.  A generator encapsulates zero or more
    58	\emph{generator iterations}.  By default, the programmer must assume
    59	that generator iterations are run in parallel in separate implicit
    60	threads unless the generators are instances of \TYP{SequentialGenerator}; the
    61	actual behavior of generators is dictated by library code, as
    62	described in \secref{defining-generators}.
    63	No generator iterations are run until the generator expression completes.
    64	For each generator iteration, a generator object produces a value or a tuple
    65	of values.  These values are bound to the identifiers to the left of the arrow,
    66	which are in scope of the subsequent generator clause list and of the
    67	body of the construct containing the generator clause list.
    68	
    69	An expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket} in a
    70	generator clause list is interpreted as a \emph{filter}.  A generator
    71	iteration is performed only if the filter yields \EXP{()}.
    72	If the filter yields no value, subsequent expressions in
    73	the generator clause list will not be evaluated.  Note in particular that \VAR{true} is a \TYP{Boolean} value yielding \EXP{()} exactly once, while \VAR{false} is a \TYP{Boolean} value that yields no elements.
    74	
    75	The order of nesting of generators need not imply anything about the
    76	relative order of nesting of iterations.  In most cases, multiple
    77	generators can be considered equivalent to multiple nested loops.
    78	However, the compiler will make an effort to choose the best possible
    79	iteration order it can for a multiple-generator loop, and may even
    80	combine generators together; there may be no such guarantee for nested
    81	loops.  Thus loops with multiple generators are preferable to distinct nested loops in general.
    82	Note that the early termination behavior of nested looping is subtly
    83	different from a single multi-generator loop, since nested loops give
    84	rise to nested thread groups; see \secref{early-termination}.
    85	
    86	Each generator iteration of the innermost generator clause
    87	corresponds to a \emph{body iteration}, or simply an \emph{iteration}
    88	of the generator clause list.  Each iteration is run in its own implicit
    89	thread.  Each expression in the generator clause list can be considered
    90	to evaluate in a separate implicit thread.  Together these implicit
    91	threads form a thread group.  Evaluation of an expression with generators
    92	completes only when this thread group has completed.
    93	
    94	Some common \TYP{Generator}s include:
    95	\begin{quote}
    96	\begin{tabular}{ll}
    97	\EXP{l\COLONOP{}u}              & Any range expression \\
    98	\EXP{a}                         & Array \VAR{a} generates its elements \\
    99	\EXP{a.\VAR{indices}}           & The index set of array \VAR{a} \\
   100	\EXP{\{0,1,2,3\}}               & The elements of an aggregate expression \\
   101	\EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)}       & A sequential version of generator \VAR{g}
   102	\end{tabular}
   103	\end{quote}
   104	The generator \EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)} forces the iterations using
   105	values from \VAR{g} to be performed in order.  Every generator has an
   106	associated \emph{natural order} which is the order obtained by
   107	\EXP{sequential}.  For example, a sequential \KWD{for} loop starting
   108	at $1$ and going to $n$ can be written as follows:
   109	%for i <- sequential(1:n) do
   110	%  \cdots
   111	%end
   112	\begin{Fortress}
   113	\(\KWD{for} i \leftarrow \VAR{sequential}(1\COLONOP{}n) \KWD{do}\)\\
   114	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \cdots\)\-\\\poptabs
   115	\(\KWD{end}\)

   118	will always nest strictly inside preceding generator clauses and
   119	outside succeeding ones.

   122	a tuple of values, which can be bound by a tuple of variables to the
   123	left of the arrow:

   127	\end{Fortress}
   128	The parallelism of a loop on this generator follows the spatial
   129	distribution (discussed in \secref{distributions})
   130	of \VAR{my2DArray} as closely as possible.

  SILENCE="golden"

fi

if [ $# -ne 1 ] ; then
  echo "Usage: fortick [-q] somefile.suffix (one file, no more, no less)"
  echo "  Replaces backtick-delimited fortress with nicely formatted fortress."
  echo "  Writes to somefile.tex (will overwrite original if suffix = \"tex\")"

fi

if grep -q "usepackage{.*fortify.*}" $1 ; then
  true
else

  fi
fi

BASENAME=${1%.*}

USE_EMACS=${USE_EMACS:-emacs}
[ -n "$EMACS" ] && unset EMACSLOADPATH
"${USE_EMACS}" -batch "$@" -l "$FORTRESS_HOME/Fortify/fortify.el" -f fortick

(* ------------------------------------------------- ⍤ the rank operator ---- *)
(* the typed readers that replace `asif` on a cell's result (u09) *)
aplScalOf(x: RR64): RR64 = x
aplNth[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\], j: ZZ32): RR64 = v[j]
aplNth2[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 = m[i,j]

(* a cell result's shape, so that a later cell of a different shape is APL's
   LENGTH ERROR rather than a wrong answer *)
aplSig(x: RR64): RR64 = -1.0
aplSig[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): RR64 = 1.0 |v|
aplSig[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): RR64 = 1.0 ((1000 aplRowsOf(m)) + aplColsOf(m))
aplSameSig(rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Boolean = do
    ok: Boolean := true
    s0 = aplSig(rs[0])
    k: ZZ32 := 1
    while k < |rs| do
        (if aplSig(rs[k]) =/= s0 then ok := false end)
        k := k + 1
    end
    ok
  end

(* assemble-by-first-result: the rank of the RESULT is read off rs[0] by
   overload resolution (u09_result.out).  aplAsm1 has a one-dimensional frame,
   aplAsm2 a two-dimensional one (f⍤1 over a rank-3 array). *)
aplAsm1From(r0: RR64, rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]
        requires { aplSameSig(rs) } =
    aplVec(|rs|, fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => aplScalOf(rs[i]))
aplAsm1From[\nat s\](r0: Vector[\RR64,s\], rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]
        requires { aplSameSig(rs) } =
    aplMat(|rs|, |r0|, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => aplNth(rs[i], j))
aplAsm1From[\nat p, nat q\](r0: Matrix[\RR64,p,q\], rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]):
        Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] requires { aplSameSig(rs) } =
    aplArr3(|rs|, aplRowsOf(r0), aplColsOf(r0),
            fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): RR64 => aplNth2(rs[i], j, k))
aplAsm1(rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Object = aplAsm1From(rs[0], rs)

aplAsm2From(r0: RR64, rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\], d0: ZZ32, d1: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]
        requires { aplSameSig(rs) } =
    aplMat(d0, d1, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => aplScalOf(rs[(i d1) + j]))
aplAsm2From[\nat s\](r0: Vector[\RR64,s\], rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\], d0: ZZ32, d1: ZZ32):
        Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] requires { aplSameSig(rs) } =
    aplArr3(d0, d1, |r0|, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): RR64 => aplNth(rs[(i d1) + j], k))
aplAsm2(rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\], d0: ZZ32, d1: ZZ32): Object = aplAsm2From(rs[0], rs, d0, d1)

(* monadic f⍤1 : the cells are the rows.  A vector IS one cell, so f⍤1 on a
   vector is f on the vector. *)
aplRank1(f: ()->Any, x: RR64): Object = aplCall1(f, x)
aplRank1[\nat s\](f: ()->Any, v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Object = aplCall1(f, v)
aplRank1[\nat r, nat c\](f: ()->Any, m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Object = do
    rows = aplRowsOf(m)
    rs = array[\Any\](rows)
    i: ZZ32 := 0
    while i < rows do
        rs[i] := aplCall1(f, AplRow[\r,c\](m, i))

    53	When used as left and right enclosing operators, $|\quad|$ computes the

   219	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downplus} and \EXP{\downminus}.
   220	
   221	The construction \EXP{x \pm y} produces the interval \EXP{\bsINT{x-y,x+y}}.
   222	
   223	\subsection{Intersection, Union, and Set Difference Operators}
   224	
   225	Sets support the operations of intersection \EXP{\cap}, union
   226	\EXP{\cup}, disjoint union \EXP{\uplus},
   227	set difference \EXP{\setminus}, and symmetric set difference
   228	\EXP{\ominus}.  Disjoint union
   229	throws \TYP{DisjointUnionError} if the arguments are in fact not disjoint.
   230	
   231	Intervals support the operations of intersection \EXP{\cap}, union
   232	\EXP{\cup}, and interior hull \EXP{\underline{\union}}.
   233	The operation \EXP{\Cap} returns a pair of intervals; if the intersection of
   234	the arguments is a single contiguous span of real numbers, then the first result is an
   235	interval representing that span and the second result is an empty interval,
   236	but if the intersection is two spans, then two (disjoint) intervals are returned.
   237	The operation \EXP{\Cup} returns a pair of intervals; if the arguments overlap, then
   238	the first result is the union of the two intervals and the second result is an empty interval,
   239	but if the arguments are disjoint, they are simply returned as is.
   240	
   241	\subsection{Minimum and Maximum Operators}
   242	
   243	The operator \OPR{MAX} returns the larger of its two operands,
   244	and \OPR{MIN} returns the smaller of its two operands.
   245	
   246	For floating-point numbers, if either argument is a \TYP{NaN} then
   247	\TYP{NaN} is returned.  The floating-point operations \OPR{MAXNUM} and
   248	\OPR{MINNUM}
   249	behave similarly except that if one argument is \TYP{NaN} and the
   250	other is a number, the number is returned.  For all four of these
   251	operators, when applied to floating-point values,
   252	\EXP{-0} is considered to be smaller than \EXP{+0}.
   253	
   254	\subsection{GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators}
   255	
   256	The infix operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common
   257	divisor of its integer operands, and \OPR{LCM} computes the least
   258	common multiple.  The operator \OPR{CHOOSE} computes binomial
   259	coefficients:
   260	\EXP{n \OPR{CHOOSE} k = \binom{n}{k} = { n! \over k!(n-k)! }}.
   261	
   262	The expression \EXP{e \neq e'} is semantically equivalent to the expression
   263	\EXP{\neg(e = e')}.
   264	
   265	
   266	\subsection{Comparisons Operators}
   267	
   268	Unless otherwise noted, the operators described in this section
   269	produce boolean (\VAR{true}/\VAR{false}) results.
   270	
   271	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and $>$ are
   272	  used for numerical comparisons
   273	and are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types.
   274	Comparison of rational values throws \TYP{RationalComparisonError}
   275	if either argument is the rational infinity \EXP{1/0} or the
   276	rational indefinite \EXP{0/0}.
   277	Comparison of floating-point values throws \TYP{FloatingComparisonError}
   278	if either argument is a \TYP{NaN}.
   279	
   280	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} may also be
   281	used to compare characters
   282	(according to the numerical value of their Unicode codepoint values)
   283	and strings (lexicographic order based on the character ordering).
   284	They also use lexicographic order when used to compare lists
   285	whose elements support these same comparison operators.
   286	
   287	When $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} are used to compare numerical
   288	intervals, the result is a boolean interval.  The functions
   289	\VAR{possibly} and \VAR{certainly} are useful for converting
   290	boolean intervals to boolean values for testing.  Thus
   291	\EXP{\VAR{possibly}(x>y)} is true if and only if there is some value in the interval
   292	\VAR{x} that is greater than some value in the interval \VAR{y}, while
   293	\EXP{\VAR{certainly}(x>y)} is true if and only if \VAR{x} and \VAR{y} are nonempty
   294	and every value in \VAR{x} is greater than every value in \VAR{y}.
   295	
   296	The operators \EXP{\subset}, \EXP{\subseteq}, \EXP{\supseteq}, and
   297	\EXP{\supset} may be used to compare sets or intervals regarded as sets.
   298	
   299	The operator \EXP{\in} may be used to test whether a value is a member of
   300	a set, list, array, interval, or range.
   301	
   302	\subsection{Logical Operators}
   303	
   304	The following binary operators may be used on boolean values:
   305	\begin{center}
   306	\begin{tabular}{rl}
   307	$\wedge$ & \scap{and} \\
   308	$\vee$ & inclusive \scap{or} \\
   309	$\underline{\vee}$ or $\oplus$ or $\neq$ & exclusive \scap{or} \\
   310	$\equiv$ or $\leftrightarrow$ or $=$ & equivalence (if and only if) \\
   311	$\rightarrow$ & \scap{implies} \\
   312	$\overline{\wedge}$ & \scap{nand} \\
   313	$\overline{\vee}$ & \scap{nor}
   314	\end{tabular}
   315	\end{center}
   316	
   317	These same operators may also be applied to boolean intervals
   318	to produce boolean interval results.
   319	
   320	The following operators may be used on integers to perform
   321	``bitwise'' operations:
   322	\begin{center}
   323	\begin{tabular}{rl}
   324	$\twointersectand$ & bitwise \scap{and} \\
   325	$\twointersector$ & bitwise inclusive \scap{or} \\
   326	$\underline{\twointersector}$ & bitwise exclusive \scap{or}
   327	\end{tabular}
   328	\end{center}
   329	The prefix operator \EXP{\twointersectnot} computes the bitwise
   330	\scap{not} of an integer.
   331	
   332	
   333	\subsection{Conditional Operators}
   334	\seclabel{standard-conditional-oprs}
   335	
   336	If \EXP{p(x)} and \EXP{q(x)} are expressions that produce
   337	boolean results, the expression \EXP{p(x) \wedge\mathpunct{\mathtt{:}}
   338	  q(x)} computes the
   339	logical \scap{and} of those two results by first evaluating \EXP{p(x)}.
   340	If the result of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{true}, then \EXP{q(x)} is also
   341	evaluated, and its
   342	result becomes the result of the entire expression; but if the result
   343	of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{false}, then \EXP{q(x)} is not evaluated,
   344	and the result of the entire expression is \VAR{false} without further ado.
   345	(Similarly, evaluating the expression \EXP{p(x)
   346	  \vee\mathpunct{\mathtt{:}} q(x)} does not
   347	evaluate \EXP{q(x)} if the result of \EXP{p(x)} is \VAR{true}.)
   348	Contrast this with the expression \EXP{p(x) \wedge q(x)} (with no colon),
   349	which evaluates both \EXP{p(x)} and \EXP{q(x)}, in no specified order and
   350	possibly in parallel.

    12	\section{Operator Fixity}
    13	\seclabel{operator-fixity}
    14	
    15	\note{Multifix operators are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	Most operators in Fortress can be used variously as prefix, postfix,
    18	infix, nofix, or multifix operators.
    19	(See \secref{chained-multifix} for a discussion of how
    20	infix operators may be chained
    21	or treated as multifix operators.)
    22	\note{
    23	Victor: I think that we shouldn't list ``multifix'' separately here.
    24	 (Note that multifix does not appear in any of the tables.)
    25	 Rather multifix is a way to interpret infix operators.}
    26	Some operators can be used in pairs
    27	as enclosing (bracketing) operators---see \secref{enclosing-ops}.
    28	The Fortress language
    29	dictates only the rules of syntax; whether an operator has
    30	a meaning when used in a particular way depends only on whether
    31	there is a definition in the program for that operator when
    32	used in that particular way (see \chapref{operatordefs}).
    33	
    34	The fixity of a non-enclosing operator is determined by context.
    35	To the left of such an operator we may find
    36	(1) a \emph{primary tail} (described below),
    37	(2) another operator, or
    38	(3) a comma, semicolon, or left encloser.  To the right we may find
    39	(1) a \emph{primary front} (described below),
    40	(2) another operator, (3) a comma, semicolon, or right
    41	encloser, or (4) a line break.
    42	%
    43	A primary tail is an identifier, a literal,
    44	a right encloser, or a superscripted postfix operator (exponent operator).
    45	A primary front is an identifier, a literal, or a left encloser.
    46	%
    47	\note{
    48	A primary expression is an identifier, a literal,
    49	an expression enclosed by matching enclosers, a field selection,
    50	or an expression followed by a postfix operator.}
    51	Considered in all combinations, this makes twelve possibilities.
    52	In some cases one must also consider whether or not whitespace separates the operator
    53	from what lies on either side.  The rules of operator fixity are specified
    54	by \figref{opr-fixity1}, where the center column indicates the fixity that results
    55	from the left and right context specified by the other columns.

    91	A case described in the center column of the table as an {\bf error}
    92	is a static error; for such cases, the fixity mentioned in parentheses
    93	is the recommended treatment of the operator for the purpose of
    94	attempting to continuing the parse in search of other errors.
    95	
    96	The table may seem complicated, but it all boils down to a couple of practical rules of thumb:
    97	\begin{enumerate}
    98	\item {\it Any} operator can be prefix, postfix, infix, or nofix.

   101	or \emph{tight} (having whitespace on neither side), but it mustn't be \emph{lopsided}

    17	Juxtaposition in Fortress may be a function call or
    18	a special infix operator.  \Library\ include several declarations of
    19	a \KWD{juxtaposition} operator.
    20	
    21	When two expressions are juxtaposed, the juxtaposition is interpreted as
    22	follows:
    23	if the left-hand-side expression is a function, juxtaposition performs
    24	function application;
    25	otherwise, juxtaposition performs the
    26	\KWD{juxtaposition} operator application.
    27	
    28	The manner in which a juxtaposition of three or more items must be associated
    29	requires type information and awareness of whitespace.  (This is an inherent property
    30	of customary mathematical notation, which Fortress is designed to emulate where feasible.)
    31	Therefore a Fortress compiler must produce a provisional parse in which such
    32	multi-element juxtapositions are held in abeyance, then perform a type analysis
    33	on each element and use that information to rewrite the n-ary juxtaposition
    34	into a tree of binary juxtapositions.
    35	
    36	All we need to know is whether each element of a
    37	juxtaposition has an arrow type.
    38	There are actually three legitimate possibilities for each element of a juxtaposition:
    39	(a) it has an arrow type, in which case it is considered to be a function
    40	element;

    42	to be a non-function element.
