    12	\chapter{Overloading and Multiple Dispatch}
    13	\chaplabel{multiple-dispatch}
    14	
    15	\note{Keyword and varargs parameters are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	Fortress allows functions and methods (collectively called \emph{functionals})
    18	to be \emph{overloaded}.  That is,
    19	there may be multiple declarations for the same functional name
    20	visible in a single scope (which may include inherited method declarations),
    21	and several of them may be applicable to any particular functional call.
    22	
    23	However, with these benefits comes the potential for ambiguous calls at run time.
    24	For an overloaded functional call,
    25	the most specific applicable declaration is chosen, if any.
    26	Otherwise, any of the applicable declarations such that
    27	no other applicable declaration is more specific than them is chosen.
    28	
    29	
    30	In this chapter, we describe how to determine which declarations
    31	are \emph{applicable} to a particular functional call,
    32	and when several are applicable, how to select among them.
    33	We also provide overloading rules for the declarations of functionals
    34	to eliminate \emph{some possibility} of ambiguous calls at run time,
    35	whether or not these calls actually appear in the program.
    36	\secref{overloading-terms} introduces some terminology and notation.
    37	In \secref{functional-applicability},
    38	we show how to determine which declarations
    39	are applicable to a \emph{named functional call}
    40	(a function call described in \secref{function-calls}
    41	or a naked method invocation described in \secref{naked-method-calls})
    42	when all declarations have only ordinary parameters
    43	(without varargs or keyword
    44	parameters).
    45	We discuss how to handle dotted method calls
    46	(described in \secref{dotted-method-calls})
    47	in \secref{dotted-method-applicability},
    48	and declarations with varargs and keyword
    49	parameters in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}.
    50	Determining which declaration is applied,
    51	if several are applicable,
    52	is discussed in \secref{resolving-overloading}.
    53	
    54	
    55	\section{Principles of Overloading}
    56	\seclabel{overloading-terms}
    57	
    58	Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
    59	be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
    60	the following shadowing rules:
    61	\begin{itemize}
    62	\item
    63	dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
    64	the same name, and
    65	\item
    66	dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
    67	or object expression
    68	shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
    69	provided by a different trait or object declaration
    70	or object expression.
    71	\end{itemize}
    72	Also, note that a trait or object declaration
    73	or object expression must not have a
    74	functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
    75	same name, either directly or by inheritance.
    76	Therefore, top-level functions can overload
    77	with other top-level functions and functional methods,
    78	dotted methods with other dotted methods,
    79	and functional methods with other functional methods and top-level functions.
    80	It is a static error if any top-level function declaration is
    81	more specific than any functional method declaration.
    82	If a top-level function declaration is overloaded with a functional method
    83	declaration, the top-level function declaration must not be more specific than
    84	the functional method declaration.
    85	
    86	
    87	Operator declarations with the same name but different fixity
    88	are not a valid overloading; they are unambiguous declarations.
    89	An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
    90	(described in \secref{opr-ident})
    91	of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
    92	declarations in the same component.
    93	Therefore, such an operator method declaration
    94	must satisfy the overloading rules
    95	(described in \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
    96	with every operator declaration in the same component.
    97	
    98	\note{This restriction will be relaxed.}
    99	
   100	Although there may be multiple declarations
   101	with the same functional name,
   102	it is an error for their static parameters to differ
   103	(up to $\alpha$-equivalence),
   104	or for one declaration to have static parameters
   105	and another to not have them.
   106	Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
   107	declarations are applicable,
   108	so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
   109	
   110	
   111	
   112	Recall from \chapref{types} that we write
   113	$T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
   114	and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$.
   115	
   116	
   117	\section{Applicability to Named Functional Calls}
   118	\seclabel{functional-applicability}
   119	In this section, we show how to determine which declarations are
   120	applicable to a named functional call when all declarations have only
   121	ordinary parameters (i.e., neither varargs nor keyword parameters).
   122	
   123	For the purpose of defining applicability, a named functional call can
   124	be characterized by the name of the functional and its argument type.
   125	Recall that a functional has a single parameter, which may be a tuple
   126	(a dotted method has a receiver as well).
   127	 We abuse notation by using
   128	\emph{static call $\f(\As)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   129	name $\f$ and whose argument has static type $\As$, and
   130	\emph{dynamic call $\f(\Xs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   131	We use \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
   132	name $\f$ and whose argument, when evaluated, has dynamic type $\Cs$.
   133	(Note that if the type system is sound---and we certainly hope that
   134	it is!---then $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \As$ for all well-typed calls to $\f$.)
   135	We use the term \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to static and dynamic calls
   136	collectively.
   137	We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
   138	have been instantiated or inferred.
   139	
   140	
   141	We also use \emph{function declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$} to refer to a
   142	function declaration with function name $\f$, parameter type $\Ps$,
   143	and return type $\Us$.
   144	
   145	
   146	For method declarations, we must take into account the self parameter,
   147	as follows:
   148	
   149	A \emph{dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps):\Us$} is a dotted
   150	method declaration with name $f$, where $\Ps_0$ is the trait or object
   151	type in which the declaration appears, $\Ps$ is the parameter type,
   152	and $\Us$ is the return type.  (Note that despite the suggestive
   153	notation, a dotted method declaration does not explicitly list its
   154	self parameter.)
   155	
   156	A \emph{functional method declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$ with self
   157	parameter at $i$} is a functional method declaration with name $f$,
   158	with the parameter \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}} in the $i$th position
   159	of the parameter type $\Ps$, and return type $\Us$.  Note that the static
   160	type of the self parameter is the trait or object trait type in which
   161	the declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$ occurs.  In the following, we will use
   162	$\Ps_i$ to refer to the $i$th element of $\Ps$.
   163	
   164	We elide the return type of a declaration, writing $\f(\Ps)$ and
   165	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$, when the return type is not relevant to the
   166	discussion.
   167	Note that static parameters may appear in the types $\Ps_0$, $\Ps$, and $\Us$.
   168	
   169	
   170	A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable} to a call $\f(\Cs)$
   171	if the call is in the scope of the declaration and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   172	(See \chapref{names} for the definition of scope.)
   173	If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters,
   174	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   175	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   176	
   177	
   178	
   179	Note that a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ may invoke a dotted method
   180	declaration if the declaration is provided by the trait or object
   181	enclosing the call.  To account for this, let $\Cs_0$ be the trait or
   182	object declaration immediately enclosing the call.
   184	Then we consider a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ as $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$
   185	if $\Cs_0$ provides dotted method declarations applicable to $\f(\Cs)$, and
   186	use the rule for applicability to dotted method calls (described in
   187	\secref{dotted-method-applicability}) to determine which declarations
   188	are applicable to $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$.
   189	
   190	
   191	
   192	\section{Applicability to Dotted Method Calls}
   193	\seclabel{dotted-method-applicability}
   194	
   195	Dotted method applications can be characterized similarly to named
   196	functional applications, except that, analogously to dotted method declarations,
   197	we use $\Cs_0$ to denote the dynamic type of the receiver object,
   198	and, as for named functional calls, $\Cs$ to denote the dynamic
   199	type of the argument of a  dotted method call.
   200	We write $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ to refer to the  call.
   201	
   202	A dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable}
   203	to a dotted method call $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype
   204	\Ps_0$ and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   205	If the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ include static parameters,
   206	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   207	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   208	
   209	
   210	
   211	\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
   212	\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}
   213	
   214	The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
   215	parameters is that we
   216	can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
   217	though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
   218	set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
   219	these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
   220	of arguments that can be passed to it.
   221	
   222	
   223	A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
   224	number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
   225	passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
   226	number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
   227	called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
   228	will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
   229	arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
   230	simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
   231	implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
   233	For example, the following declaration:
   235	\begin{Fortress}
   236	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
   237	\end{Fortress}
   238	would be expanded into:
   244	\begin{Fortress}
   245	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   246	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   247	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   248	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   249	\(\ldots\)
   250	\end{Fortress}
   251	A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
   252	any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.
   253	
   254	
   255	
   256	\section{Overloading Resolution}
   257	\seclabel{resolving-overloading}
   258	
   259	\note{
   260	Victor: Does this paragraph, other than the last sentence,
   261	really belong in this section?}
   262	
   263	To evaluate a given functional call,
   264	it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
   265	to dispatch to.
   266	To do so,
   267	we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
   268	If there is exactly one such declaration,
   269	then the call dispatches to that declaration.
   270	If there is no such declaration,
   271	then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
   272	(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
   273	for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
   274	If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
   275	then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
   276	no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
   277	
   278	
   279	
   280	We use the subtype relation to compare parameter types to determine
   281	a more specific declaration.
   282	Formally, a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than a declaration
   283	$\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.  Similarly, a declaration
   284	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is more specific than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$
   285	if $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$ and $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.
   286	(See \secref{resolving-coercion} for how coercion
   287	changes the definition of ``more specific''.)
   288	Restrictions on the definition of overloaded functionals
   289	(see \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
   290	guarantee that among all applicable declarations,
   291	one is more specific than all the others.
   292	If the declarations include static parameters,
   293	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   294	before comparing their parameter types
   295	to determine which declaration is more specific.

   159	of the parameter type $\Ps$, and return type $\Us$.  Note that the static
   160	type of the self parameter is the trait or object trait type in which
   161	the declaration $\f(\Ps):\Us$ occurs.  In the following, we will use
   162	$\Ps_i$ to refer to the $i$th element of $\Ps$.
   163	
   164	We elide the return type of a declaration, writing $\f(\Ps)$ and
   165	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$, when the return type is not relevant to the
   166	discussion.
   167	Note that static parameters may appear in the types $\Ps_0$, $\Ps$, and $\Us$.
   168	
   169	
   170	A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable} to a call $\f(\Cs)$
   171	if the call is in the scope of the declaration and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   172	(See \chapref{names} for the definition of scope.)
   173	If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters,
   174	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   175	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   176	
   177	
   178	
   179	Note that a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ may invoke a dotted method
   180	declaration if the declaration is provided by the trait or object
   181	enclosing the call.  To account for this, let $\Cs_0$ be the trait or
   182	object declaration immediately enclosing the call.
   184	Then we consider a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ as $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$
   185	if $\Cs_0$ provides dotted method declarations applicable to $\f(\Cs)$, and
   186	use the rule for applicability to dotted method calls (described in
   187	\secref{dotted-method-applicability}) to determine which declarations
   188	are applicable to $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$.
   189	
   190	
   191	
   192	\section{Applicability to Dotted Method Calls}
   193	\seclabel{dotted-method-applicability}
   194	
   195	Dotted method applications can be characterized similarly to named
   196	functional applications, except that, analogously to dotted method declarations,
   197	we use $\Cs_0$ to denote the dynamic type of the receiver object,
   198	and, as for named functional calls, $\Cs$ to denote the dynamic
   199	type of the argument of a  dotted method call.
   200	We write $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ to refer to the  call.
   201	
   202	A dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable}
   203	to a dotted method call $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype
   204	\Ps_0$ and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
   205	If the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ include static parameters,
   206	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   207	before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
   208	
   209	
   210	
   211	\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
   212	\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}
   213	
   214	The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
   215	parameters is that we
   216	can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
   217	though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
   218	set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
   219	these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
   220	of arguments that can be passed to it.
   221	
   222	
   223	A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
   224	number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
   225	passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
   226	number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
   227	called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
   228	will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
   229	arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
   230	simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
   231	implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
   233	For example, the following declaration:
   235	\begin{Fortress}
   236	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
   237	\end{Fortress}
   238	would be expanded into:
   244	\begin{Fortress}
   245	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   246	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   247	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   248	\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
   249	\(\ldots\)
   250	\end{Fortress}
   251	A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
   252	any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.
   253	
   254	
   255	
   256	\section{Overloading Resolution}
   257	\seclabel{resolving-overloading}
   258	
   259	\note{
   260	Victor: Does this paragraph, other than the last sentence,
   261	really belong in this section?}
   262	
   263	To evaluate a given functional call,
   264	it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
   265	to dispatch to.
   266	To do so,
   267	we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
   268	If there is exactly one such declaration,
   269	then the call dispatches to that declaration.
   270	If there is no such declaration,
   271	then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
   272	(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
   273	for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
   274	If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
   275	then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
   276	no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
   277	
   278	
   279	
   280	We use the subtype relation to compare parameter types to determine
   281	a more specific declaration.
   282	Formally, a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than a declaration
   283	$\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.  Similarly, a declaration
   284	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is more specific than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$
   285	if $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$ and $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.
   286	(See \secref{resolving-coercion} for how coercion
   287	changes the definition of ``more specific''.)
   288	Restrictions on the definition of overloaded functionals
   289	(see \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
   290	guarantee that among all applicable declarations,
   291	one is more specific than all the others.
   292	If the declarations include static parameters,
   293	they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
   294	before comparing their parameter types
   295	to determine which declaration is more specific.

11	
    12	\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{reduction-expr}
    14	
    15	\begin{Grammar}
    16	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
    17	\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    18	\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\
    19	
    20	\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
    21	\end{Grammar}
    22	
    23	A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
    24	$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
    25	an optional generator clause list (described in
    26	\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
    27	There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
    28	\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
    29	\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
    31	\begin{Fortress}
    32	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
    33	\end{Fortress}
    34	Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
    35	the method %generate[\R0\]
    36	\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
    37	of the trait %Generator[\T\]
    38	\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
    39	it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
    40	\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
    41	and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
    42	and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
    43	generated element and combining them using the reduction.
    44	When a generator clause
    45	list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
    46	identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
    47	body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
    48	thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
    49	combined together using \emph{Op}
    50	\label{redexpr-redvar}
    51	as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
    52	The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.
    53	When no generator clause list is provided, the body is taken to be an
    54	object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are
    55	combined.  Thus, the reduction expression \EXP{\sum a} is equivalent
    56	to \EXP{\sum\limits_{x\leftarrow{}a}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}}.
    57	
    58	A reduction expression with a generator list:
    60	\begin{Fortress}
    61	\(\sum [v_{\mathrm{1}} \gets g_{\mathrm{1}}, v_{\mathrm{2}} \gets g_{\mathrm{2}}, \ldots] e\)
    62	\end{Fortress}
    63	is equivalent to the following code:
    71	\begin{Fortress}
    72	\(\KWD{do}\)\\
    73	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{var}\:\VAR{result}\COLON \mathbb{Z}32 = 0\)\\
    74	\(  \KWD{for}\:v_{1} \leftarrow g_{1}, v_{2} \leftarrow g_{2}, \ldots \KWD{do}\)\\
    75	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{result} \mathrel{+}= e\)\-\\\poptabs
    76	\(  \KWD{end}\)\\
    77	\(  \VAR{result}\)\-\\\poptabs
    78	\(\KWD{end}\)
    79	\end{Fortress}
    80	where \VAR{result} is a fresh variable.
    82	A reduction expression without a generator clause list:
    84	\begin{Fortress}
    85	\(\sum g\)
    86	\end{Fortress}
    87	is equivalent to the following:
    89	\begin{Fortress}
    90	\(\sum [x \gets g] x\)
    91	\end{Fortress}
    92	Note that reduction expressions without generator clause lists can be used to
    93	conveniently sum any aggregate expression (described in
    94	\secref{aggregate-expr}), since every aggregate expression
    95	is a generator.

    11	
    12	\section{Generators}
    13	\seclabel{generators}
    14	
    15	\note{Distributions are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\begin{Grammar}
    18	\emph{GeneratorClauseList} &::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding}(\EXP{,} \emph{GeneratorClause})$^*$ \\
    19	
    20	\emph{GeneratorBinding}
    21	&::=& \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}\EXP{\leftarrow}\emph{Expr} \\
    22	
    23	\emph{GeneratorClause}
    24	&::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding} \\
    25	&$|$& \emph{Expr} \\
    26	
    27	\emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}
    28	&::=& \emph{BindId}\\
    29	&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}\EXP{,} \emph{BindIdList} \texttt{)}\\
    30	
    31	\emph{BindIdList} &::=& \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^*$\\
    32	
    33	\emph{BindId} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
    34	&$|$& \KWD{\_}\\
    35	\end{Grammar}
    36	
    37	Fortress makes extensive use of comma-separated \emph{generator clause lists}
    38	to express parallel iteration.  Generator clause lists occur in
    39	generated expressions (described in \secref{generated}) and
    40	\KWD{for} loops (described in \secref{for-expr}),
    41	sums and big operators (described in \secref{reduction-expr}),
    42	and comprehensions (described in \secref{comprehensions}).
    43	We refer to these
    44	collectively as \emph{expressions with generator clauses}.  Every expression with
    45	generator clauses contains a \emph{body expression} which is evaluated for each
    46	combination of values bound in the generator clause list
    47	(each such combination yields an \emph{iteration} of the body).
    48	
    49	A generator clause is either a \emph{generator binding} or
    50	an expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket}
    51	(this includes the type \TYP{Boolean}).
    52	A generator clause list must begin with a generator binding.
    53	A generator binding consists of one or more
    54	comma-separated identifiers followed by the token \EXP{\leftarrow},
    55	followed by a subexpression (called the \emph{generator expression}).
    56	A generator expression evaluates to an object whose type is
    57	\TYP{Generator}.  A generator encapsulates zero or more
    58	\emph{generator iterations}.  By default, the programmer must assume
    59	that generator iterations are run in parallel in separate implicit
    60	threads unless the generators are instances of \TYP{SequentialGenerator}; the
    61	actual behavior of generators is dictated by library code, as
    62	described in \secref{defining-generators}.
    63	No generator iterations are run until the generator expression completes.
    64	For each generator iteration, a generator object produces a value or a tuple
    65	of values.  These values are bound to the identifiers to the left of the arrow,
    66	which are in scope of the subsequent generator clause list and of the
    67	body of the construct containing the generator clause list.
    68	
    69	An expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket} in a
    70	generator clause list is interpreted as a \emph{filter}.  A generator
    71	iteration is performed only if the filter yields \EXP{()}.
    72	If the filter yields no value, subsequent expressions in
    73	the generator clause list will not be evaluated.  Note in particular that \VAR{true} is a \TYP{Boolean} value yielding \EXP{()} exactly once, while \VAR{false} is a \TYP{Boolean} value that yields no elements.
    74	
    75	The order of nesting of generators need not imply anything about the
    76	relative order of nesting of iterations.  In most cases, multiple
    77	generators can be considered equivalent to multiple nested loops.
    78	However, the compiler will make an effort to choose the best possible
    79	iteration order it can for a multiple-generator loop, and may even
    80	combine generators together; there may be no such guarantee for nested
    81	loops.  Thus loops with multiple generators are preferable to distinct nested loops in general.
    82	Note that the early termination behavior of nested looping is subtly
    83	different from a single multi-generator loop, since nested loops give
    84	rise to nested thread groups; see \secref{early-termination}.
    85	
    86	Each generator iteration of the innermost generator clause
    87	corresponds to a \emph{body iteration}, or simply an \emph{iteration}
    88	of the generator clause list.  Each iteration is run in its own implicit
    89	thread.  Each expression in the generator clause list can be considered
    90	to evaluate in a separate implicit thread.  Together these implicit
    91	threads form a thread group.  Evaluation of an expression with generators
    92	completes only when this thread group has completed.
    93	
    94	Some common \TYP{Generator}s include:
    95	\begin{quote}
    96	\begin{tabular}{ll}
    97	\EXP{l\COLONOP{}u}              & Any range expression \\
    98	\EXP{a}                         & Array \VAR{a} generates its elements \\
    99	\EXP{a.\VAR{indices}}           & The index set of array \VAR{a} \\
   100	\EXP{\{0,1,2,3\}}               & The elements of an aggregate expression \\
   101	\EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)}       & A sequential version of generator \VAR{g}
   102	\end{tabular}
   103	\end{quote}
   104	The generator \EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)} forces the iterations using
   105	values from \VAR{g} to be performed in order.  Every generator has an
   106	associated \emph{natural order} which is the order obtained by
   107	\EXP{sequential}.  For example, a sequential \KWD{for} loop starting
   108	at $1$ and going to $n$ can be written as follows:
   112	\begin{Fortress}
   113	\(\KWD{for} i \leftarrow \VAR{sequential}(1\COLONOP{}n) \KWD{do}\)\\
   114	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \cdots\)\-\\\poptabs
   115	\(\KWD{end}\)
   116	\end{Fortress}
   117	The \VAR{sequential} generator respects generator clause list ordering; it
   118	will always nest strictly inside preceding generator clauses and
   119	outside succeeding ones.
   120	
   121	Given a multidimensional array, the \VAR{indices} generator returns
   122	a tuple of values, which can be bound by a tuple of variables to the
   123	left of the arrow:
   125	\begin{Fortress}
   126	\((i,j) \leftarrow \VAR{my2DArray}.\VAR{indices}\)
   127	\end{Fortress}
   128	The parallelism of a loop on this generator follows the spatial
   129	distribution (discussed in \secref{distributions})
   130	of \VAR{my2DArray} as closely as possible.

    11	
    12	\section{Comprehensions}
    13	\seclabel{comprehensions}
    14	
    15	\note{Array comprehensions are not yet supported.
    16	
    17	Array comprehensions do not have to be comprehensive --
    18	may not define a value for every cell.
    19	When an unitialized array cell is accessed, an uncaught exception is raised.}
    20	
    21	\begin{Grammar}
    22	\emph{Comprehension}
    23	&::=&
    24	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \texttt{[} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    25	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause}$^+$ \texttt{]}\\
    26	&$|$&
    27	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \{ \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    28	\emph{Entry} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \} \\
    29	&$|$& \option{\KWD{BIG}} \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    30	\emph{Expr} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \emph{RightEncloser} \\
    31	
    32	\emph{Entry} &::=& \emph{Expr} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr} \\
    33	
    34	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause} &::=&
    35	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList}\\
    36	
    37	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} &::=&
    38	\emph{IdOrInt} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
    39	&$|$& \texttt( \emph{IdOrInt}\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrIntList} \texttt) \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
    40	
    41	\emph{IdOrInt} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
    42	&$|$& \emph{IntLiteralExpr}\\
    43	
    44	\emph{IdOrIntList} &::=& \emph{IdOrInt}(\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrInt})$^*$ \\
    45	\end{Grammar}
    46	
    47	Fortress provides \emph{comprehension} syntax, in which a generator clause list
    48	binds values used in the body expression on the left-hand side of the
    49	token \EXP{|}.  As described in \secref{generators}, each iteration of
    50	the body expression must be assumed to execute in its own implicit
    51	thread.  Comprehensions evaluate to aggregate values and have
    52	corresponding aggregate types.  The rules for evaluation of a
    53	comprehension are similar to those for a reduction expression (see
    54	\secref{reduction-expr}).
    55	
    56	The relationship between a comprehension and an aggregate expression (\secref{aggregate-expr}) is similar to the relationship between a reduction expression (\secref{reduction-expr}) and the corresponding infix operator application (\secref{operator-app-expr}).  The language does not enforce an explicit connection between comprehension syntax and the corresponding aggregate syntax, but in practice libraries that provide definitions for aggregate expressions are expected to define a corresponding comprehension and \emph{vice versa}.  As with reduction expressions, a comprehension using a particular set of enclosers corresponds to a call to a \emph{big bracketing operator}.  Thus the definition of set comprehensions is given by a function with the following signature:
    58	\begin{Fortress}
    59	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}} \{\llbracket{}T\rrbracket g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0}\}\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
    60	\end{Fortress}
    61	This is almost identical to the signature required to define a reduction
    62	expression \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}}, shown in \secref{reduction-expr}.
    63	Further information on defining comprehensions are described
    64	in \secref{defining-generators}.
    65	
    66	A set comprehension is enclosed in braces, with a left-hand body
    67	separated by the token \EXP{|} from a generator clause list.
    68	For example, the comprehension:
    69	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.SetComp.tex}
    70	evaluates to the set
    71	\begin{Fortress}
    72	\(\{0, 4, 16\}\)
    73	\end{Fortress}
    74	
    75	Map comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
    76	except that the left-hand body must be of the form
    77	\EXP{e_{1} \mapsto e_{2}}.
    78	If \EXP{e_{1}} produces the same value but \EXP{e_{2}} a different value on more
    79	than one iteration of the generator list,
    80	a \TYP{KeyOverlap} exception is thrown.
    81	For example:
    82	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.MapComp.tex}
    83	evaluates to the map
    84	\begin{Fortress}
    85	\(\{0 \mapsto 0, 4 \mapsto 8, 16 \mapsto 64\}\)
    86	\end{Fortress}
    87	
    88	
    89	List comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
    90	except that they are syntactically enclosed in angle brackets.
    91	For example:
    92	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.ListComp.tex}
    93	evaluates to the list
    94	\begin{Fortress}
    95	\(\langle 0, 4, 16 \rangle\)
    96	\end{Fortress}
    97	Note that the order of elements in the resulting list corresponds to
    98	the \emph{natural order} of the generators in the generator clause
    99	list (see \secref{defining-generators}).
   100	
   101	Array comprehensions are like set comprehensions, except that they are
   102	syntactically enclosed in brackets, and the left-hand body must be of
   103	the form \txt{($\mathit{index}_1$, $\mathit{index}_2$, \ldots,
   104	  $\mathit{index}_n$) $\mapsto$ $\mathit{e}$}.  Moreover an array
   105	comprehension may have multiple clauses separated by semicolons or
   106	line breaks.  Each clause conceptually corresponds to an independent loop.
   107	Clauses are run in order.  The result is an $n$-dimensional array.
   108	For example:
   109	\begin{Fortress}
   110	\(a = [\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\((x,y,1) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}\)\\
   111	\(      (1,y,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
   112	\(      (x,1,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
   113	\(      (x,y,z) \mapsto x+y\cdot z \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\,]\)\-\\\poptabs
   114	\end{Fortress}
===== expressions/operator-app.tex =====
    11	
    12	\section{Operator Applications}
    13	\seclabel{operator-app-expr}
    14	
    15	\note{Examples/discussion of juxtaposition as an operator.
    16	
    17	Should be a static check that an applicable declaration exists.
    18	}
    19	
    20	\begin{Grammar}
    21	\emph{OpExpr}
    22	&::=& \emph{EncloserOp} \option{\emph{OpExpr}} \option{\emph{EncloserOp}} \\
    23	&$|$& \emph{OpExpr} \emph{EncloserOp} \option{\emph{OpExpr}} \\
    24	&$|$& \emph{Primary}\\
    25	
    26	\emph{EncloserOp} &::=& \emph{Encloser}\\
    27	&$|$& \emph{Op}\\
    28	
    29	\emph{Primary}
    30	&::=& \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \option{\emph{ExprList}} \emph{RightEncloser} \\
    31	&$|$& \emph{Primary} \verb+^+ \emph{Exponent}\\
    32	&$|$& \emph{Primary} \emph{ExponentOp}\\
    33	
    34	\emph{Exponent}
    35	&::=& \emph{Id}\\
    36	&$|$& \emph{ParenthesisDelimited}\\
    37	&$|$& \emph{LiteralExpr}\\
    38	&$|$& \KWD{self}\\
    39

    13	\seclabel{reduction-expr}

    15	\begin{Grammar}
    16	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&

    18	\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\

    21	\end{Grammar}

    23	A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
    24	$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
    25	an optional generator clause list (described in
    26	\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
    27	There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
    28	\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
    29	\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
    31	\begin{Fortress}
    32	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
    33	\end{Fortress}
    34	Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
    35	the method %generate[\R0\]
    36	\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
    37	of the trait %Generator[\T\]
    38	\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
    39	it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
    40	\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
    41	and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
    42	and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
    43	generated element and combining them using the reduction.
    44	When a generator clause
    45	list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
    46	identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
    47	body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
    48	thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
    49	combined together using \emph{Op}
    50	\label{redexpr-redvar}

    12	\section{Generators}
    13	\seclabel{generators}
    14	
    15	\note{Distributions are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\begin{Grammar}
    18	\emph{GeneratorClauseList} &::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding}(\EXP{,} \emph{GeneratorClause})$^*$ \\
    19	
    20	\emph{GeneratorBinding}
    21	&::=& \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}\EXP{\leftarrow}\emph{Expr} \\
    22	
    23	\emph{GeneratorClause}
    24	&::=& \emph{GeneratorBinding} \\
    25	&$|$& \emph{Expr} \\
    26	
    27	\emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple}
    28	&::=& \emph{BindId}\\
    29	&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}\EXP{,} \emph{BindIdList} \texttt{)}\\
    30	
    31	\emph{BindIdList} &::=& \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^*$\\
    32	
    33	\emph{BindId} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
    34	&$|$& \KWD{\_}\\
    35	\end{Grammar}
    36	
    37	Fortress makes extensive use of comma-separated \emph{generator clause lists}
    38	to express parallel iteration.  Generator clause lists occur in
    39	generated expressions (described in \secref{generated}) and
    40	\KWD{for} loops (described in \secref{for-expr}),
    41	sums and big operators (described in \secref{reduction-expr}),
    42	and comprehensions (described in \secref{comprehensions}).
    43	We refer to these
    44	collectively as \emph{expressions with generator clauses}.  Every expression with
    45	generator clauses contains a \emph{body expression} which is evaluated for each
    46	combination of values bound in the generator clause list
    47	(each such combination yields an \emph{iteration} of the body).
    48	
    49	A generator clause is either a \emph{generator binding} or
    50	an expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket}
    51	(this includes the type \TYP{Boolean}).
    52	A generator clause list must begin with a generator binding.
    53	A generator binding consists of one or more
    54	comma-separated identifiers followed by the token \EXP{\leftarrow},
    55	followed by a subexpression (called the \emph{generator expression}).
    56	A generator expression evaluates to an object whose type is
    57	\TYP{Generator}.  A generator encapsulates zero or more
    58	\emph{generator iterations}.  By default, the programmer must assume
    59	that generator iterations are run in parallel in separate implicit
    60	threads unless the generators are instances of \TYP{SequentialGenerator}; the
    61	actual behavior of generators is dictated by library code, as
    62	described in \secref{defining-generators}.
    63	No generator iterations are run until the generator expression completes.
    64	For each generator iteration, a generator object produces a value or a tuple
    65	of values.  These values are bound to the identifiers to the left of the arrow,
    66	which are in scope of the subsequent generator clause list and of the
    67	body of the construct containing the generator clause list.
    68	
    69	An expression of type \EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket()\rrbracket} in a
    70	generator clause list is interpreted as a \emph{filter}.  A generator
    71	iteration is performed only if the filter yields \EXP{()}.
    72	If the filter yields no value, subsequent expressions in
    73	the generator clause list will not be evaluated.  Note in particular that \VAR{true} is a \TYP{Boolean} value yielding \EXP{()} exactly once, while \VAR{false} is a \TYP{Boolean} value that yields no elements.
    74	
    75	The order of nesting of generators need not imply anything about the
    76	relative order of nesting of iterations.  In most cases, multiple
    77	generators can be considered equivalent to multiple nested loops.
    78	However, the compiler will make an effort to choose the best possible
    79	iteration order it can for a multiple-generator loop, and may even
    80	combine generators together; there may be no such guarantee for nested
    81	loops.  Thus loops with multiple generators are preferable to distinct nested loops in general.
    82	Note that the early termination behavior of nested looping is subtly
    83	different from a single multi-generator loop, since nested loops give
    84	rise to nested thread groups; see \secref{early-termination}.
    85	
    86	Each generator iteration of the innermost generator clause
    87	corresponds to a \emph{body iteration}, or simply an \emph{iteration}
    88	of the generator clause list.  Each iteration is run in its own implicit
    89	thread.  Each expression in the generator clause list can be considered
    90	to evaluate in a separate implicit thread.  Together these implicit
    91	threads form a thread group.  Evaluation of an expression with generators
    92	completes only when this thread group has completed.
    93	
    94	Some common \TYP{Generator}s include:
    95	\begin{quote}
    96	\begin{tabular}{ll}
    97	\EXP{l\COLONOP{}u}              & Any range expression \\
    98	\EXP{a}                         & Array \VAR{a} generates its elements \\
    99	\EXP{a.\VAR{indices}}           & The index set of array \VAR{a} \\
   100	\EXP{\{0,1,2,3\}}               & The elements of an aggregate expression \\
   101	\EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)}       & A sequential version of generator \VAR{g}
   102	\end{tabular}
   103	\end{quote}
   104	The generator \EXP{\VAR{sequential}(g)} forces the iterations using
   105	values from \VAR{g} to be performed in order.  Every generator has an
   106	associated \emph{natural order} which is the order obtained by
   107	\EXP{sequential}.  For example, a sequential \KWD{for} loop starting
   108	at $1$ and going to $n$ can be written as follows:
   112	\begin{Fortress}
   113	\(\KWD{for} i \leftarrow \VAR{sequential}(1\COLONOP{}n) \KWD{do}\)\\
   114	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \cdots\)\-\\\poptabs
   115	\(\KWD{end}\)
   116	\end{Fortress}
   117	The \VAR{sequential} generator respects generator clause list ordering; it
   118	will always nest strictly inside preceding generator clauses and
   119	outside succeeding ones.
   120	
   121	Given a multidimensional array, the \VAR{indices} generator returns
   122	a tuple of values, which can be bound by a tuple of variables to the
   123	left of the arrow:
   125	\begin{Fortress}
   126	\((i,j) \leftarrow \VAR{my2DArray}.\VAR{indices}\)
   127	\end{Fortress}
   128	The parallelism of a loop on this generator follows the spatial
   129	distribution (discussed in \secref{distributions})
   130	of \VAR{my2DArray} as closely as possible.

    12	\section{Comprehensions}
    13	\seclabel{comprehensions}
    14	
    15	\note{Array comprehensions are not yet supported.
    16	
    17	Array comprehensions do not have to be comprehensive --
    18	may not define a value for every cell.
    19	When an unitialized array cell is accessed, an uncaught exception is raised.}

    21	\begin{Grammar}
    22	\emph{Comprehension}
    23	&::=&
    24	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \texttt{[} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    25	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause}$^+$ \texttt{]}\\
    26	&$|$&
    27	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \{ \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    28	\emph{Entry} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \} \\
    29	&$|$& \option{\KWD{BIG}} \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    30	\emph{Expr} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \emph{RightEncloser} \\
    31	
    32	\emph{Entry} &::=& \emph{Expr} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr} \\
    33	
    34	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause} &::=&
    35	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList}\\
    36	
    37	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} &::=&
    38	\emph{IdOrInt} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
    39	&$|$& \texttt( \emph{IdOrInt}\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrIntList} \texttt) \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
    40	
    41	\emph{IdOrInt} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
    42	&$|$& \emph{IntLiteralExpr}\\
    43	
    44	\emph{IdOrIntList} &::=& \emph{IdOrInt}(\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrInt})$^*$ \\
    45	\end{Grammar}
    46	
    47	Fortress provides \emph{comprehension} syntax, in which a generator clause list
    48	binds values used in the body expression on the left-hand side of the
    49	token \EXP{|}.  As described in \secref{generators}, each iteration of
    50	the body expression must be assumed to execute in its own implicit
    51	thread.  Comprehensions evaluate to aggregate values and have
    52	corresponding aggregate types.  The rules for evaluation of a
    53	comprehension are similar to those for a reduction expression (see
    54	\secref{reduction-expr}).
    55	
    56	The relationship between a comprehension and an aggregate expression (\secref{aggregate-expr}) is similar to the relationship between a reduction expression (\secref{reduction-expr}) and the corresponding infix operator application (\secref{operator-app-expr}).  The language does not enforce an explicit connection between comprehension syntax and the corresponding aggregate syntax, but in practice libraries that provide definitions for aggregate expressions are expected to define a corresponding comprehension and \emph{vice versa}.  As with reduction expressions, a comprehension using a particular set of enclosers corresponds to a call to a \emph{big bracketing operator}.  Thus the definition of set comprehensions is given by a function with the following signature:
    58	\begin{Fortress}
    59	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}} \{\llbracket{}T\rrbracket g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0}\}\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
    60	\end{Fortress}
    61	This is almost identical to the signature required to define a reduction
    62	expression \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}}, shown in \secref{reduction-expr}.
    63	Further information on defining comprehensions are described
    64	in \secref{defining-generators}.
    65	
    66	A set comprehension is enclosed in braces, with a left-hand body
    67	separated by the token \EXP{|} from a generator clause list.
    68	For example, the comprehension:
    69	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.SetComp.tex}
    70	evaluates to the set
    71	\begin{Fortress}
    72	\(\{0, 4, 16\}\)
    73	\end{Fortress}
    74	
    75	Map comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
    76	except that the left-hand body must be of the form
    77	\EXP{e_{1} \mapsto e_{2}}.
    78	If \EXP{e_{1}} produces the same value but \EXP{e_{2}} a different value on more
    79	than one iteration of the generator list,
    80	a \TYP{KeyOverlap} exception is thrown.
    81	For example:
    82	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.MapComp.tex}
    83	evaluates to the map
    84	\begin{Fortress}
    85	\(\{0 \mapsto 0, 4 \mapsto 8, 16 \mapsto 64\}\)
    86	\end{Fortress}
    87	
    88	
    89	List comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
    90	except that they are syntactically enclosed in angle brackets.
    91	For example:
    92	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.ListComp.tex}
    93	evaluates to the list
    94	\begin{Fortress}
    95	\(\langle 0, 4, 16 \rangle\)
    96	\end{Fortress}
    97	Note that the order of elements in the resulting list corresponds to
    98	the \emph{natural order} of the generators in the generator clause
    99	list (see \secref{defining-generators}).
   100	
   101	Array comprehensions are like set comprehensions, except that they are
   102	syntactically enclosed in brackets, and the left-hand body must be of
   103	the form \txt{($\mathit{index}_1$, $\mathit{index}_2$, \ldots,
   104	  $\mathit{index}_n$) $\mapsto$ $\mathit{e}$}.  Moreover an array
   105	comprehension may have multiple clauses separated by semicolons or
   106	line breaks.  Each clause conceptually corresponds to an independent loop.
   107	Clauses are run in order.  The result is an $n$-dimensional array.
   108	For example:
   109	\begin{Fortress}
   110	\(a = [\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\((x,y,1) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}\)\\
   111	\(      (1,y,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
   112	\(      (x,1,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
   113	\(      (x,y,z) \mapsto x+y\cdot z \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\,]\)\-\\\poptabs
   114	\end{Fortress}

\section{Operator Precedence and Associativity}
\seclabel{operator-precedence}

Fortress specifies that certain operators have higher precedence than
certain other operators and certain operators are associative,
so that one need not use parentheses in all
cases where operators are mixed in an expression.  (See
\appref{operator-precedence} for a detailed description of operator
precedence and associativity in Fortress.)  However, Fortress
does not follow the practice of other programming languages in
simply assigning an integer to each operator and then saying that
the precedence of any two operators can be compared by comparing
their assigned integers.  Instead, Fortress relies on defining traditional
groups of operators based on their meaning and shape, and specifies
specific precedence relationships between some of these groups.
If there is no specific precedence relationship between two
operators, then parentheses must be used.  For example, Fortress
does not accept the expression \EXP{a + b \cup c};
one must write either \EXP{(a + b) \cup c} or \EXP{a + (b \cup c)}.
(Whether or not the result then makes any sense depends on what definitions
have been made for the \EXP{+} and \EXP{\cup} operators---see
\chapref{operatordefs}.)

Here are the basic principles of operator precedence and associativity
in Fortress:

\begin{itemize}
\item
Member selection (\txt{.}) and method invocation
(\EXP{.\VAR{name}(\ldots)}) are not operators.  They have higher precedence
than any operator listed below.

\item
Subscripting (\txt{[ ]} and any kind of subscripting operators,
which can be any kind of enclosing operators),
superscripting (\txt{{\char'136}}),
and postfix operators have higher precedence than any operator
listed below; within this group, these operations are left-associative
(performed left-to-right).

\item
\emph{Tight juxtaposition}, that is, juxtaposition without intervening
whitespace, has higher precedence than any operator listed below.  The
associativity of tight juxtaposition is type-dependent;
see \secref{juxtameaning}.

\item
Next, \emph{tight fractions}, that is,
the use of the operator `\EXP{/}' with no whitespace on either side,
have higher precedence than any operator listed below.
The tight-fraction operator has no precedence compared with itself,
so it is not permitted to be used more than once in a tight fraction
without use of parentheses.

\item
\emph{Loose juxtaposition}, that is, juxtaposition with intervening
whitespace, has higher precedence than any operator listed below.  The
associativity of loose juxtaposition is type-dependent and is
different from that for tight juxtaposition; see \secref{juxtameaning}.
Note that \emph{lopsided juxtaposition}
(having whitespace on one side but not the other) is a static error as
described in \secref{operator-fixity}.


\item
Prefix operators have higher precedence than any operator listed below.
However, it is a static error for an operand of a loose prefix operator
to be an operand of a tight infix operator.

\item
The infix operators are partitioned into certain traditional groups, as
explained below.  They have higher precedence than any operator listed below.

\item
The equal symbol `\EXP{=}' in binding context,
the assignment operator `\EXP{\ASSIGN}', and
compound assignment operators (\EXP{\mathrel{+}=}, \EXP{-=}, \EXP{\wedge=},
\EXP{\vee=}, \EXP{\cap=}, \EXP{\cup=}, and so on as described in
\secref{operator-app-expr})
have lower precedence than any operator listed above.
Note that compound assignment operators themselves are not operator names.
\end{itemize}

The infix binary operators are divided into four general categories: arithmetic,
relational, boolean, and other.  The arithmetic operators are further categorized as
multiplication/division/intersection, addition/subtraction/union, and other.
The relational operators are further categorized as equivalence,
inequivalence, ordering, and other.
The boolean operators
are further categorized as conjunctive, disjunctive, and other.

The arithmetic and relational operators are further divided into groups based on shape:
\begin{itemize}
\item ``ordinary'' operators:
\EXP{+ - \cdot \times / \pm \mp \oplus \ominus
\odot \otimes \oslash
\boxplus \boxminus \boxdot \boxtimes < \leq \geq > \ll \lll \ggg \gg
\nless \nleq \ngeq \ngtr} etc.

The arithmetic operations in this group are further subdivided into
``plain'' (\EXP{+ - \cdot \times / \pm \mp} etc.),
``circled'' (\EXP{\oplus \ominus \odot \otimes \oslash} etc.),
``boxed'' (\EXP{\boxplus \boxminus \boxdot \boxtimes} etc.), and so on;
 any of these groups may be used with
the plain relational operators
(\EXP{< \leq \geq > \ll \lll \ggg \gg \nless \nleq \ngeq \ngtr} etc.),
but the groups might not be mixed.

\item ``rounded horseshoe'' or ``set'' operators:
\EXP{\cap \Cap \cup \Cup \uplus \subset \subseteq \supseteq \supset
\Subset \Supset \not\subset \nsubseteq \nsupseteq \not\supset}  etc.

\item ``square horseshoe'' operators:
\EXP{\sqcap \sqcup \sqsubset \sqsubseteq \sqsupseteq \sqsupset
\not\sqsubseteq \not\sqsupseteq} etc.

\item ``curly'' operators:
\EXP{\curlywedge \curlyvee \prec \preceq \succeq \succ
\nprec \not\preccurlyeq \not\succcurlyeq \nsucc} etc.

\item ``triangular'' relations:
\EXP{\lhd \unlhd \unrhd \rhd
\ntriangleleft \ntrianglelefteq \ntrianglerighteq \ntriangleright} etc.

\item ``chickenfoot'' relations: \EXP{<\!\llap{-} \rlap{-}\!>} etc.
\end{itemize}
The principles of precedence for binary operators are then as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item
A multiplication or division or intersection operator has higher precedence than any addition or subtraction or union
operator that is in the same shape group.

\item Certain addition and subtraction operators come in pairs,
such as \EXP{+} and \EXP{-}, or \EXP{\oplus} and \EXP{\ominus},
 which are considered to have the
same precedence and so may be mixed within an expression and are grouped
left-associatively.  These addition-subtraction pairs are the \emph{only}
cases where two different operators are considered to have the same precedence.

\item An arithmetic operator has higher precedence than any equivalence or inequivalence operator.

\item An arithmetic operator has higher precedence than any relational operator that is in the same shape group.

\item A relational operator has higher precedence than any boolean operator.

\item A conjunctive boolean operator has higher precedence than any disjunctive boolean operator.
\end{itemize}

While the rules of precedence are complicated, they
are intended to be both unsurprising and conservative.
Note that operator precedence in Fortress is not always transitive;
for example,  while \EXP{+} has higher precedence than \EXP{<}
(so you can write \EXP{a~+~b~<~c} without parentheses), and \EXP{<} has higher precedence than
\EXP{\vee} (so you can write \EXP{a~<~b~\vee~c~<~d} without
parentheses), it is \emph{not} true
that \EXP{+} has higher precedence than \EXP{\vee}---the expression
\EXP{a~\vee~b~+~c} is not permitted,
and one must instead write \EXP{(a~\vee~b)~+~c} or \EXP{a~\vee~(b~+~c)}.

Another point is that the various multiplication and division operators
do \emph{not} have ``the same precedence''; they may not be mixed freely with each other.
For example, one cannot write
\EXP{u~\cdot~v~\times~w};
one must write \EXP{(u~\cdot~v)~\times~w} or (more likely)
\EXP{u~\cdot~(v~\times~w)}.
Similarly, one cannot write
\EXP{a~\odot~b~/~c~\odot~d};
but juxtaposition
does bind more tightly than a loose (whitespace-surrounded) division
slash, so one is allowed to write \EXP{a~b~/~c~d}, and this means the
same as \EXP{(a~b)/(c~d)}.
On the other hand, loose juxtaposition binds less tightly than a tight
division slash,
so that \EXP{a~b/c~d} means the same as \EXP{a~(b/c)~d}.  On the other
other hand,
tight juxtaposition binds more tightly than tight division, so that
\EXP{(n+1)/(n+2)(n+3)}
means the same as \EXP{(n+1)/((n+2)(n+3))}.

There are two additional rules intended to catch misleading code:
it is a static error for an operand of a tight infix or tight prefix operator
to be a loose juxtaposition, and
it is a static error if the rules of precedence determine that a use
of infix operator \VAR{a} has higher or equal precedence
than a use of infix operator \VAR{b}, but that particular use of
\VAR{a} is loose  and that particular
use of \VAR{b} is tight.  Thus, for example, the expression
\EXP{\sin~x~+~y} is permitted, but \EXP{\sin~x\!+\!y} is not permitted.
Similarly, the expression \EXP{a~\cdot~b~+~c} is permitted,
as are \EXP{a{\cdot}b~+~c} and \EXP{a{\cdot}b\!+\!c}, but
\EXP{a~\cdot~b\!+\!c} is not permitted.
(The rule detects only the presence or absence of whitespace, not the
amount of whitespace,
so \EXP{a~~~\cdot~b~+~c} is permitted.  You have to draw the line somewhere.)

When in doubt, just use parentheses.  If there's a problem, the compiler will (probably) let you know.

trait Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2\]
    extends { Indexed1[\s0\], Indexed2[\s1\], Indexed3[\s2\], Rank3,
              StandardMutableArrayType[\Array3[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\],T,
                                        (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] }
    excludes { Number, String }

    getter size():ZZ32 = s0 s1 s2
    getter sizes():(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32) = (s0, s1, s2)
    getter bounds():CompactFullRange3D[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
        sized3Range[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32\](0,0,0,b0,b1,b2,s0,s1,s2)

    getter asString():String = do
      r : String := "[" b0 "#" s0 "," b1 "#" s1 "," b2 "#" s2 "]"
      row(i,k) =
          for j <- seq(0#s1) do
            r := r " " self[b0+i,b1+j,b2+k]
          end
      plane(k) =
        if s1 > 0 then
          row(0,k)
          for i <- seq(1#(s0-1)) do
            r := r // " "
            row(i,k)
          end
        end
      if s0=0 then
        r "[]"
      else
        r := r // "["
        plane(0)
        for k <- seq(1#(s2-1)) do
          r := r " ;;" //  " "
          plane(k)
        end
        r " ]"
      end
    end

    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0 s1 s2
...
    map[\R\](f:T->R): Array3[\R,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\] =
        replica[\R\]().fill(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):R =>
                                f(get(i-b0,j-b1,k-b2)))
    ivmap[\R\](f:((ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32),T)->R): Array3[\R,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\] =
        replica[\R\]().fill(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):R =>
                                f((i,j,k),get(i-b0,j-b1,k-b2)))

    freeze():ImmutableArray[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
        fail("Freeze not defined yet!")
end

(** hoisted out here to work around absence of type inference for methods. **)
__subarray[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2,
            nat bo0, nat so0, nat bo1, nat so1, nat bo2, nat so2,
            nat o0, nat o1, nat o2\]
      (this:Array3[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\],
       _:N[\bo0\],_:N[\so0\],_:N[\bo1\],_:N[\so1\],_:N[\bo2\],_:N[\so2\],
       _:N[\o0\],_:N[\o1\],_:N[\o2\], m0:ZZ32,m1:ZZ32,m2:ZZ32): Array3[\T,bo0,so0,bo1,so1,bo2,so2\] =
    this.subarray[\bo0,so0,bo1,so1,bo2,so2,o0,o1,o2\](m0,m1,m2)

object __DefaultArray3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2\]() extends
                                        Array3[\T, b0, s0, b1, s1, b2, s2\]
  mem:PrimitiveArray[\T,(s0 (s1 s2))\] = PrimitiveArray[\T,(s0 (s1 s2))\]()

  ofs(i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):ZZ32 = (i s1 + j) s2 + k

  init0(t:(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = mem.init0(ofs(t),v)
  put(t:(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), v:T) : () = mem.put(ofs(t),v)
  get(t:(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)) : T = mem.get(ofs(t))
end

(** Simple 3-D subarray, used when we have no other knowledge of the
    underlying structure.  If we're on top of a PrimitiveArray we can
    really do much better than this.
    (b0,b1,b2)#(s0,s1,s2) are the bounds of the subarray.
    (bu0,bu1,bu2)#(su0,su1,su2) are the bounds of the underlying array.
    m_i, o_i are multiplier and offset (0-based) of dimension i.
**)
object SubArray3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2,
                     nat bu0, nat su0, nat bu1, nat su1, nat bu2, nat su2\]
                (mem: Array3[\T,bu0,su0,bu1,su1,bu2,su2\],

trait Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2\]
    extends { Indexed1[\s0\], Indexed2[\s1\], Indexed3[\s2\], Rank3,
              StandardMutableArrayType[\Array3[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1,b2,s2\],T,
                                        (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] }
    excludes { Number, String }

    getter size():ZZ32 = s0 s1 s2
    getter sizes():(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32) = (s0, s1, s2)
    getter bounds():CompactFullRange3D[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
        sized3Range[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32\](0,0,0,b0,b1,b2,s0,s1,s2)

    getter asString():String = do
      r : String := "[" b0 "#" s0 "," b1 "#" s1 "," b2 "#" s2 "]"
      row(i,k) =
          for j <- seq(0#s1) do
            r := r " " self[b0+i,b1+j,b2+k]
          end
      plane(k) =
        if s1 > 0 then
          row(0,k)
          for i <- seq(1#(s0-1)) do

        end
      if s0=0 then

      else
        r := r // "["
        plane(0)

        end

      end

1. **Chained subscripting / indexed power** — ours classified `m[i][j] → (m[i])[j]` as a *design limit* ("grammatical by design in the spec"); Astra and the blinded run called it an *interpreter gap*. **Astra and blinded are right** (rows 1-3): `concrete-syntax.tex:944-950` is left-recursive on `Primary`, `precedence.tex:44-51` puts subscripting and superscripting in one left-associative group, and `Expression.rats` parses both. 2. **`f()[i]`** — blinded called it a grammar/design limit, and the review's correction of row 1 risked sweeping it in. **Blinded is right** (row 4): `juxtameaning.tex:157-161` makes it a static error and the interpreter quotes that sentence. 3. **"The library cannot call the user's `opr +`"** — our sum experiment stated it unconditionally. **Falsified as stated** (rows 30-32): it holds for top-level `opr` declarations, not for functional methods. The important half is that the fallback is *silent*.
4. **`do … end` as a comprehension body** — blinded listed it as unavailable. **Falsified** (row 10).
5. **Transpose** — Astra recorded `transpose(W)` as a word and a remaining departure; the blinded run avoided needing it. **Ours is right** (row 34): the spec's postfix `^T` is declarable and runs.
6. **Both juxtaposition directions** — Astra judged `v M` unavailable; ours reached it via `Rank1 excludes Rank2`; blinded reached it with two plain overloads on unrelated object types. **Blinded's route is the simpler correct one** (row 33); `excludes` is needed only when the carriers share a supertype.
7. **`extends Number`** — Astra and ours agree it is illegal per `traits.tex:228-235`; ours adds that the walk path never enforces it and that the library types then work in full (rows 22, 52). Not a disagreement, a merge: the row needs both halves or it misleads.

10. **Matrix pasting** — run-b (and its independent worker) recorded that matrix pasting fails, `[ A ; B ]` included; run-b2 recorded that a rank-one paste always fails but a rank-two paste of square blocks works. **Both are half right** (rows 106, 107): a grid with a single row *or* a single column of matrix elements always fails the extent check — `g18` settles the stacked `[ A ; B ]` of square blocks that run-b never reached and its worker inferred — while a 2×2 grid of square blocks pastes correctly and a 2×2 grid of non-square blocks throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. The neighbouring rejection of a `property` after a method *is* an implementation gap (row 125), because the same grammar puts `PropertyDecl` in both groups.

aplCall(f: Any, l: Any, r: Any): Any = do
    AplFrames.push(f, l, r)
    (* the pop is in a finally so that a contract violation inside the body
       (APL's VALUE ERROR on ⍺, a LENGTH ERROR) leaves no stale frame behind *)
    try f() finally AplFrames.pop() end
  end
aplCall1(f: Any, r: Any): Any = aplCall(f, AplNoAlpha, r)
aplHasAlpha(): Boolean = typecase AplFrames.topA() of AplNoAlpha => false; else => true end
(* APL's VALUE ERROR for ⍺ in a monadic call, as a contract violation *)
aplAlpha(): Any requires { aplHasAlpha() } = AplFrames.topA()
aplOmega(): Any = AplFrames.topO()
aplSelf(): Any = AplFrames.topF()
(* ⍺ ← e : sets ⍺ only when it is absent, so a second ⍺ ← has no effect *)
aplDefaultAlpha(e: Any): () = if NOT aplHasAlpha() then AplFrames.setA(e) end

**implementation gap**, localised to one argument-list call in the evaluator.

reassociation procedure (`juxtameaning.tex:156-162`) makes it a static error, and

exp[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => exp(e))

nth[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\], j: ZZ32): RR64 = v[j]

(* the four vector-level functions of the model, no subscripts *)
rmsn[\nat s\](x: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsRms + (SUM[t <- x] t^2) / (|x|))
sm[\nat s\](z: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX[t <- z] t)); e / (SUM[t <- e] t) end
rmsn_b[\nat s, nat t\](dy: Vector[\RR64,s\], x: Vector[\RR64,t\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    r = SQRT (epsRms + (SUM[u <- x] u^2) / (|x|))
    y = x / r
    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / (|y|))) / r
  end
sm_b[\nat s, nat t\](p: Vector[\RR64,s\], dy: Vector[\RR64,t\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))

(* (a) collect and stack; the rank of the result is decided by the first result *)
stack(r0: RR64, rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = vec(|rs|, fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => rs[i])
stack[\nat s\](r0: Vector[\RR64,s\], rs: Array[\Any,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    mat(|rs|, |r0|, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => nth(rs[i], j))
rowsA[\nat r, nat c\](f: Any, m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Any = do
    (n, d) = m.sizes
    rs = array[\Any\](n).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): Any => f(row(m, i)))
    stack(rs[0], rs)
  end
rowsA[\nat r, nat c, nat p, nat q\](f: Any, a: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], b: Matrix[\RR64,p,q\]): Any = do
    (n, d) = a.sizes
    rs = array[\Any\](n).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): Any => f(row(a, i), row(b, i)))
    stack(rs[0], rs)
  end
(* (b) a parallel for over the rows, writing through row views of a preallocated matrix *)
rowsB[\nat r, nat c\](f: Any, m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
    (n, d) = m.sizes
    out = zerosM(n, d)
    for i <- 0#n do row(out, i).assign(f(row(m, i))) end
    out
  end
rowsB[\nat r, nat c, nat p, nat q\](f: Any, a: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], b: Matrix[\RR64,p,q\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
    (n, d) = a.sizes
    out = zerosM(n, d)
    for i <- 0#n do row(out, i).assign(f(row(a, i), row(b, i))) end
    out
  end
(* (c) a comprehension over the rows and a builder that stacks the list *)
stackL(r0: RR64, rs: List[\Any\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = vec(|rs|, fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => rs[i])
stackL[\nat s\](r0: Vector[\RR64,s\], rs: List[\Any\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    mat(|rs|, |r0|, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => nth(rs[i], j))
rowsC[\nat r, nat c\](f: Any, m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Any = do
    (n, d) = m.sizes
    rs = <|[\Any\] f(row(m, i)) | i <- 0#n |>
    stackL(rs[0], rs)
  end

showM[\nat r, nat c\](name: String, m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): () = do
    (rows, cols) = m.sizes
    println name " " rows "x" cols
    for i <- seq(0#rows) do
        line: String := "  "
        for j <- seq(0#cols) do line := line " " m[i,j] end
        println line
    end
  end

run(): () = do
    x = mat(3, 4, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 (i + j) - 1.5)
    showM("x", x)
    println "rmsn of row 1 directly: " (rmsn(row(x, 1)))
    showM("(a) rowsA(rmsn, x)", rowsA(rmsn, x))
    showM("(b) rowsB(rmsn, x)", rowsB(rmsn, x))
    showM("(c) rowsC(rmsn, x)", rowsC(rmsn, x))
    showM("(a) rowsA(sm, x)", rowsA(sm, x))
    dy = mat(3, 4, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 0.5 - 0.25 j)
    showM("(a) rowsA(rmsn_b, dy, x)", rowsA(rmsn_b, dy, x))
    showM("(b) rowsB(rmsn_b, dy, x)", rowsB(rmsn_b, dy, x))
    showM("(a) rowsA(sm_b, rowsA(sm, x), dy)", rowsA(sm_b, rowsA(sm, x), dy))
    (* a scalar-valued row function decides a vector result in (a) and (c) *)
    println "(a) rowsA(fn r => SUM[t <- r] t, x) = " (rowsA(fn (r: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): RR64 => SUM[t <- r] t, x))
    println "(c) rowsC(fn r => SUM[t <- r] t, x) = " (rowsC(fn (r: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): RR64 => SUM[t <- r] t, x))
    (* cost on the model's shape: 64 x 16, ten repetitions each *)
    big = mat(64, 16, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 ((7 i + 3 j) MOD 11) - 5.0)
    t0 = nanoTime()
    for k <- seq(0#10) do ignore(rowsA(rmsn, big)) end
    t1 = nanoTime()
    for k <- seq(0#10) do ignore(rowsB(rmsn, big)) end
    t2 = nanoTime()
    for k <- seq(0#10) do ignore(rowsC(rmsn, big)) end
    t3 = nanoTime()
    println "10 x rmsn over 64x16: (a) " ((t1 - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms  (b) " ((t2 - t1) DIV 1000000) " ms  (c) " ((t3 - t2) DIV 1000000) " ms"
  end
end
EOF

(* q02b_arrow: can the lift's function parameter carry an arrow type, and can
   an overloaded nat-generic function (rmsn) be passed as that argument? *)
component q02b_arrow
export Executable

epsRms: RR64 = 10.0^(-5)
vec(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> RR64): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(f)
mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).fill(f)
opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => e / s)
object Row[\nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32) extends Vector[\RR64,c\]
    get(j: ZZ32): RR64 = base.get(i, j)
    put(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.put((i, j), x)
    init0(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.init0((i, j), x)
    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,c\] = array1[\U,c\]()
end
row[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = Row[\r,c\](m, i)
nth[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\], j: ZZ32): RR64 = v[j]
rmsn[\nat s\](x: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsRms + (SUM[t <- x] t^2) / (|x|))

rows[\nat r, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
    (n, d) = m.sizes
    rs = array[\Any\](n).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): Any => f(row(m, i)))
    mat(n, d, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => nth(rs[i], j))
  end

run(): () = do
    x = mat(3, 4, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 (i + j) - 1.5)
    println "(1) via a fn wrapper: " (rows(fn (r: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] => rmsn(r), x))
    println "(2) the generic function itself: " (rows(rmsn, x))
  end
end

(* q04a_varargs: the gradient as one ravel-and-catenate of nine matrices,
   the Dyalog's ⊃,/,¨ -- a varargs function over runtime-typed matrices;
   and the spelling of a transposed operand: a^T b without parentheses, and
   a parenthesised call (f(x))^T (row 144 forbids f(x)^T). *)
component q04a_varargs
export Executable

vec(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> RR64): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(f)
mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).fill(f)
zeros(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.0)
opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = m.t()

flat(ms: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]...): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    out = zeros(SUM[m <- ms] |m|)
    off: ZZ32 := 0
    for m <- seq(ms) do
        (r, c) = m.sizes
        for i <- 0#r, j <- 0#c do out[off + i c + j] := m[i,j] end
        off += r c
    end
    out
  end
onehot(ks: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], width: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    mat(|ks|, width, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if ks[i] = j then 1.0 else 0.0 end)

run(): () = do
    a = mat(2, 3, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 (3 i + j))
    b = mat(2, 2, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 10.0 + 2 i + j)
    println "(1) flat(a, b) = " (flat(a, b))
    println "(2) |flat(a, b, a)| = " (|flat(a, b, a)|)
    println "(3) a^T b = " (a^T b)
    println "(4) (a^T) b = " ((a^T) b)
    ks = array[\ZZ32\](3).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 2 i)
    dx = mat(3, 2, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 (i + j))
    println "(5) (onehot(ks, 5))^T dx = " ((onehot(ks, 5))^T dx)
  end
end

cat > q04c_gather.fss <<'EOF'
(* q04c_gather: the key vocabulary generic in the element type, so the same
   gather serves the RR64 weight views and the ZZ32 corpus matrix: gather of
   rows, a block of columns as a view, its ravel as a vector view, the one-hot
   and the validity mask from integer keys. *)
component q04c_gather
export Executable
import NatReflect.{...}

mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).fill(f)

gather[\T extends Number, nat r, nat c, nat k\](m: Matrix[\T,r,c\], ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\]): Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
    (rows, cols) = m.sizes
    array[\T\](|ks|, cols).fill(fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): T => m[ks[i], j])
  end
gather[\T extends Number, nat s, nat k\](v: Vector[\T,s\], ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\]): Array[\T,ZZ32\] =
    array[\T\](|ks|).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): T => v[ks[i]])

object Block[\T extends Number, nat br, nat bc, nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\T,br,bc\], r0: ZZ32, c0: ZZ32)
        extends Matrix[\T,r,c\]
    get(ij:(ZZ32,ZZ32)): T = do (i,j) = ij; base.get(r0 + i, c0 + j) end
    put(ij:(ZZ32,ZZ32), x: T): () = do (i,j) = ij; base.put((r0 + i, c0 + j), x) end
    init0(ij:(ZZ32,ZZ32), x: T): () = do (i,j) = ij; base.init0((r0 + i, c0 + j), x) end
    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,c\] = array2[\U,r,c\]()
end
blockOf[\T extends Number, nat br, nat bc, nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\T,br,bc\], r0: ZZ32, c0: ZZ32, _: N[\r\], _: N[\c\]): Matrix[\T,r,c\] =
    Block[\T,br,bc,r,c\](base, r0, c0)
block[\T extends Number, nat br, nat bc\](base: Matrix[\T,br,bc\], r0: ZZ32, c0: ZZ32, rows: ZZ32, cols: ZZ32): Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    blockOf(base, r0, c0, reflect(rows), reflect(cols))

(* row-major ravel of a matrix as a vector view *)
object Ravel[\T extends Number, nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\T,r,c\]) extends Vector[\T, r c\]
    get(k: ZZ32): T = base.get(k DIV c, k MOD c)
    put(k: ZZ32, x: T): () = base.put((k DIV c, k MOD c), x)
    init0(k: ZZ32, x: T): () = base.init0((k DIV c, k MOD c), x)
    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,r c\] = array1[\U,r c\]()
end
ravel[\T extends Number, nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\T,r,c\]): Array[\T,ZZ32\] = Ravel[\T,r,c\](m)

onehot[\nat k\](ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\], width: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    mat(|ks|, width, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if ks[i] = j then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
valid[\nat k\](lens: Vector[\ZZ32,k\], width: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    mat(|lens|, width, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j < lens[i] then 1.0 else 0.0 end)

run(): () = do
    tokm = array[\ZZ32\](4, 5).fill(fn (d: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 10 d + j)
    lens = array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(fn (d: ZZ32): ZZ32 => d + 1)
    b = array[\ZZ32\](2).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 3 - 2 i)
    r = gather(tokm, b)
    println "(1) gather(tokm, b) = " r
    ids = ravel(block(r, 0, 0, 2, 4))
    tg = ravel(block(r, 0, 1, 2, 4))
    println "(2) ids = " ids "  |ids| = " (|ids|)
    println "(3) tg = " tg
    println "(4) gather(lens, b) = " (gather(lens, b))
    vm = ravel(valid(gather(lens, b), 4))
    println "(5) vm = " vm "  SUM = " (SUM[t <- vm] t)
    w = mat(5, 2, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 (2 i + j))
    keys = array[\ZZ32\](3).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 4 - i)
    println "(6) gather(w, keys) = " (gather(w, keys))
    oh = onehot(keys, 5)
    println "(7) onehot(keys, 5) = " oh
    println "(8) (oh.t()) DOT gather(w, keys) = " ((oh.t()) DOT (gather(w, keys)))
    println "(9) ravel(w) DOT ravel(w) = " ((ravel(w)) DOT (ravel(w)))
  end
end
EOF
